One nuance in the auditor's favour but worth noting: the extractor's default `range_batch_size` is 3500, equal to the production range width, so at defaults it also processes one monolithic batch — but it never holds the complex cube (memmap) and the batch size is a tunable config knob, whereas the metrics stage has no such knob at all. The `ContrastEstimator` chunk loop itself is harmless overhead (chunk-sized redundant abs+astype copies); the real cost is the un-mmapped load plus the three-to-five full-size cubes that follow.

title: _load_batch makes three redundant full-batch copies of the tomogram chunk on the hot path
description: `np.array(tomogram_mmap[...])` materialises the whole complex chunk in RAM before `np.abs` allocates the float32 result, and the trailing `.astype(np.float32)` (default `copy=True`) copies that result a second time even though `np.abs` of complex64 is already float32. One line later, `raw.transpose(2, 1, 0).reshape(r_c * Az, H)` cannot return a view, so `reshape` already returns a fresh contiguous array and the appended `.copy()` duplicates it again. At the default `range_batch_size=3500` a batch is effectively the entire scene, so this turns a single needed allocation into ~4x peak memory on the prefetch thread, which also holds the next batch. Note the sibling loader in `pipelines/processing/param_extraction/metrics.py:152` correctly uses `astype(..., copy=False)`.
evidence:
raw   = np.abs(np.array(tomogram_mmap[:, :, r_start:r_end])).astype(np.float32)
        raw   = ProfilePreprocessor.apply(raw, self.threshold_factor, self.truncation_index)

        pf     = raw.transpose(2, 1, 0).reshape(r_c * Az, H).copy()
suggested_fix: Use `raw = np.abs(tomogram_mmap[:, :, r_start:r_end])` (already float32) and drop the trailing `.copy()` from the reshape, or replace it with `np.ascontiguousarray(...)` if contiguity must be guaranteed.
verdict_notes:
Reproduced every mechanical assertion from source and measured them with the project's own numpy (2.4.3, Dune env) on the real test cube /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/test_data/data/tomogram_full.npy (shape (150, 1000, 500), complex64).

Line 184 (/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/pipelines/processing/param_extraction/sigma/extractor.py):
  raw = np.abs(np.array(tomogram_mmap[:, :, r_start:r_end])).astype(np.float32)
- tomogram_mmap[:, :, r_start:r_end] is basic slicing on a np.memmap, so it is a lazy view; np.array(...) forces a full 8N-byte complex materialisation before np.abs even starts.
- np.abs of complex64 already yields float32 (verified), and np.abs of a memmap slice returns a plain ndarray in numpy 2.x (verified: type is numpy.ndarray, not numpy.memmap), so the subclass-avoidance rationale for the np.array() wrapper does not hold either.
- .astype(np.float32) defaults to copy=True (verified), so it duplicates the already-float32 abs result.
- tracemalloc on a 200-bin batch (N = 3e7): current expression peaks at 360.0 MB; np.abs(mmap_slice).astype(np.float32, copy=False) peaks at 120.0 MB and is bitwise identical (np.array_equal True). 3x transient peak for the identical result.

Line 187: pf = raw.transpose(2, 1, 0).reshape(r_c * Az, H).copy()
- raw is C-contiguous (H, Az, r_c); after transpose(2,1,0) the merge of the leading (r_c, Az) axes is stride-incompatible (needs stride[0] == Az*stride[1], i.e. 4 == Az*r_c*4), so reshape must copy. Verified: the reshape result does not share memory with raw and is already C_CONTIGUOUS.
- tracemalloc on (150, 1000, 200) float32: with the trailing .copy() peak is 240.0 MB, without it 120.0 MB, same final 120 MB resident. The .copy() is pure duplication; downstream use (pf.max(axis=1), pf/scale, _pad_rows' ascontiguousarray) needs nothing it provides, and `del raw` on line 193 means even a hypothetical view (the r_c == 1 degenerate case) would cost no more.

Sibling comparison holds: pipelines/processing/param_extraction/metrics.py:152 uses .astype(np.float32, copy=False), i.e. the lean form is the codebase's own idiom.

Path: _load_batch is submitted to the single-worker load_pool at extractor.py:395/409 and prefetches batch n+1 while batch n is fitting, so the loader's transients coexist with the live batch's pf+norm. Default range_batch_size is 3500 in both configuration/param_extraction.py:85 and :177, so for realistic crops a batch is the whole scene and this single statement sets the process RSS ceiling. No test encodes the copy semantics (grep for copy/shares_memory in tests/processing/test_param_extraction.py is empty), so the lean rewrite is safe.

Not one of the KNOWN NON-ISSUES.
correction: Numbers should be tightened. Measured transient peak is 3x (not ~4x) on line 184 — 360 MB vs 120 MB for a 200-bin batch — because the 8N complex temporary is released when np.abs returns, before .astype allocates; line 187's .copy() is a separate 2x on that statement. The claim's "reshape cannot return a view" is right for the general case but has one degenerate exception (r_c == 1, where the leading unit axis makes the merge stride-valid); that does not change the conclusion since `del raw` follows. A second instance of the same astype-without-copy=False pattern exists at pipelines/processing/param_extraction/metrics.py:41 (ContrastEstimator.run) and should be fixed in the same pass. Severity should be minor rather than major: correctness is unaffected, this is an offline extraction loop that executes a handful of times per job (ceil(R/3500) batches), not a training step or per-request handler, and for the known 1000x500 crop the waste is 900 MB vs 300 MB. It only becomes an OOM risk on much larger scenes.

title: Best-K selection denormalises the full amplitude array for every K and every lambda but keeps only the selected rows
description: `amps_out = amps_norm * scale_all[:, None]` builds a full `(N_act, k_max)` array and the very next lines use only `amps_out[idx]`, where `idx` is the (usually small) subset of pixels whose best model order is K. `select()` is called once per lambda and the loop runs k_max times, so at the default sweep (5 lambdas x k_max 5) this is 25 full-size multiplications plus 25 fancy-index copies per range batch; with a batch of ~12.6M active pixels each is ~250 MB. This runs inside the single-threaded scoring pool that the extractor explicitly instruments as a bottleneck (`_throttle_scorings` and the "GPU idle on scoring backlog" warning at extractor.py:426). The float64 promotion of `mse_all` in `score()` (line 24) and of `penalised_all` (line 41) doubles memory for the same arrays before they are cast back to float32 for storage.
evidence:
amps_out = amps_norm * scale_all[:, None]
            idx      = np.where(mask)[0]

            best_params[np.ix_(idx, list(range(0, K * 3, 3)))] = amps_out  [idx]
suggested_fix: Compute `idx` first and denormalise only the selected rows: `idx = np.where(mask)[0]; amps_out = amps_norm[idx] * scale_all[idx, None]`, then assign `amps_out` directly.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. In pipelines/processing/param_extraction/sigma/selection.py:45-57, the K loop computes `amps_out = amps_norm * scale_all[:, None]` over all N_act rows, while the only consumer is `amps_out[idx]` on line 55 where `idx` is the subset whose best model order is K. The sibling arrays `mus` and `final_sigs` are indexed directly from gpu_results, so only the amplitude branch materialises a full-size intermediate. Summed over K the code does 15*N_act multiplications where at most 5*N_act (typically ~2-3*N_act) are used, plus ~750 MB of transient allocation per select() call at N_act ~ 12.6M. Since the product does not depend on lambda_k, it is recomputed identically for every lambda in the sweep. The fix (`amps_norm[idx] * scale_all[idx, None]`) is bit-identical float32 arithmetic and no test binds the intermediate. The float64 point is also real: mse_all (line 24) and penalised_all (line 41) are promoted to float64 only to add lambda_k*K and argmin, then cast back to float32 on return (line 64), doubling traffic on (N_act, k_max) arrays for no numeric benefit. The stated context is accurate too: select() is called per lambda inside _score_and_store, which runs in a max_workers=1 score_pool that the extractor explicitly throttles (MAX_PENDING_SCORINGS=2, _throttle_scorings at extractor.py:357) and instruments with the "GPU idle on scoring backlog" warning at extractor.py:426. This is the inner loop of the extraction job, not a cold path.
correction: Details are overstated in three ways. (1) `amps_out[idx]` is NOT a full-size copy - it copies only the selected rows, which is work that must happen regardless; only the multiplication is full-size, and only the K=k_max iteration reaches ~250 MB (smaller K are proportionally smaller). (2) The default sweep is fit_lambda_values=[1e-2] (one lambda) with three fit_modes, i.e. 15 full-size multiplies per range batch, not 25; five lambdas is a user-chosen sweep, not the default. (3) The waste is a modest slice of the scoring stage: _score_and_store already allocates and writes an (n_total, 3*k_max) params array, two NaN-filled (n_total, k_max) diagnostics arrays, a fancy-index scatter and three strided reshape().transpose() writes per lambda - several GB of traffic against ~1.5 GB for the amps temporaries - and that whole stage overlaps a GPU Adam fit of 3000 steps over k_max model orders that dominates wall time by orders of magnitude. Real, trivially fixable waste (subset before multiplying, and keep mse/penalised in float32), but not a major cost driver.

title: Autoencoder and unrolled inference loaders materialise multi-GB arrays they never use
description:
Both non-backbone loaders reuse `Cropper.load_split` through the backbone `RunLoader` and pull in arrays that the pipeline discards.

1. `ImageAeRunLoader.load` calls the inherited `RunLoader._build_dataset`, which unconditionally passes `load_tomogram=True` (pipelines/backbone/inference/loader.py:143). `Cropper._load_tomogram` does `np.ascontiguousarray(np.abs(tomogram[:, az, rg]).astype(np.float32))` — the full elevation x azimuth x range cube for the split, logged by the cropper itself in GB. `ImageAeRunLoader.load` binds the result to `_arrays` and throws it away; the image autoencoder never touches curves.

2. `UnrolledRunLoader._region_ground_truth` (pipelines/unrolled/inference/loader.py:85) calls `cropper.load_split(region)`, which runs `_stack_inputs` and builds the whole primary+secondaries+interferograms stack (again GB-scale per the cropper's own log line) plus the DEM, while only `arrays["parameters"]` is used.

On a full FSAR split this is several GB of pointless I/O and RAM per inference job.
suggested_fix: Give `RunLoader._build_dataset` a `load_tomogram` flag (default True for the backbone, False for the image AE), and give `Cropper` a targets-only entry point (or call `_load_targets` directly) for the unrolled loader so the input stack and tomogram are never materialised.
verdict_notes:
Both halves of the claim reproduce exactly from source.

PART 1 — image autoencoder loads the tomogram and throws it away.
- /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/pipelines/backbone/inference/loader.py:143 hard-codes `arrays = cropper.load_split(region, load_tomogram=True)`. This is the only `load_tomogram=True` call site in the repo (grep over all .py); the parameter otherwise defaults to False.
- `Cropper._load_tomogram` (pipelines/backbone/dataset/spatial.py:84-86) does `np.ascontiguousarray(np.abs(tomogram[:, az_slice, rg_slice]).astype(np.float32))` — a materialised elevation x azimuth x range float32 cube for the split.
- `ImageAeRunLoader.load` (pipelines/image_autoencoder/inference/loader.py:72) binds the fifth return value to `_arrays` and never uses it; the returned `ImageAeRun` dataclass (lines 18-32) has no field for it, and `PatchDataset` is constructed only from `inputs`, `parameters`, `dem` (backbone loader lines 155-167). Grep for `tomogram` / `full_curves` across pipelines/image_autoencoder/ returns zero hits, and pipelines/image_autoencoder/inference/pipeline.py touches only `run.normalizer`, `run.split_name`, `run.split_region`. The auditor's "the image autoencoder never touches curves" is accurate.

PART 2 — unrolled loads the full input stack and uses only parameters.
- pipelines/unrolled/inference/loader.py:85 `arrays = cropper.load_split(region)` runs `_stack_inputs`, which allocates `np.empty((1 + n_secondaries + n_interferograms, az, rg), complex64)` and copies primary + secondaries + interferograms into it, plus `_load_targets` which also materialises the DEM.
- Only `arrays["parameters"]` is consumed (line 88). `UnrolledRun` carries `gt_parameters` and `kz_field` only, and `UnrolledPredictor` synthesises measurements from gt_parameters + kz via `MeasurementSynthesiser` (pipelines/unrolled/inference/predictor.py:53-58) — the real SAR stack is never used.
- The repo already demonstrates the correct pattern: `ParameterCropper.load_split` in pipelines/profile_autoencoder/dataset/splitting.py loads only the parameters artifact for exactly this reason, which argues the two sites are an oversight rather than a deliberate design.

MAGNITUDE (measured on the shipped test_data crop, 1000x500): tomogram_full is (150, 1000, 500) complex64 = 600 MB, materialised as abs->float32 = 300 MB at full extent; the input stack is 57 planes complex64 = 228 MB versus parameters at 30 MB. Production FSAR crops are larger. Inference fans out one worker process per run directory over GPU jobs (main/inference/_inference_entry.py + InferenceScheduler), so several concurrent workers each pay the redundant allocation.

No test covers either loader's array loading (no test file references `ImageAeRunLoader` or `UnrolledRunLoader`), so nothing encodes the current behaviour as intended.
correction:
Two details to adjust.

1. Severity. The waste is real but sits on a once-per-inference-process load path, not a training step, per-epoch loop, or per-request handler. It costs startup wall-clock and peak host RAM, never correctness, and the array is freed as soon as `load` / `_region_ground_truth` returns (nothing retains it). Under the "inefficiency counts when it runs often" bar this is a startup-cost cleanup, so minor rather than major. It is still worth fixing since the fix is trivial: thread a `load_tomogram` flag through `RunLoader._build_dataset` (default False, True only for the backbone/dual path that populates `Run.full_curves`), and give the unrolled loader a parameters-only load like the existing `ParameterCropper`.

2. "Several GB of pointless I/O". The arrays are opened with `np.load(..., mmap_mode="r")` and immediately sliced to the split region, so the I/O is the split's bytes, not the whole artifact. On the 1000x500 test crop that is up to 300 MB (tomogram, image AE) and 228 MB (input stack, unrolled) at full extent; a single split is a fraction of that. "Several GB" holds only at full production crop size, not universally.

3. The claim's file/line anchors are correct: pipelines/image_autoencoder/inference/loader.py:72, pipelines/backbone/inference/loader.py:143, pipelines/unrolled/inference/loader.py:85.

title: Autoencoder inference holds the whole split in memory and then duplicates it in float64
description:
`AeReconstructionPredictor.run_inference` concatenates gt, pred and embeddings for the entire split into float32 arrays, and `AeMetricsBase.__init__` immediately upcasts all three to float64 while the float32 originals stay alive (they are still referenced by `result`, which the pipeline keeps for the plots).

For the profile autoencoder the default inference config is `pixel_subsample = 1.0`, so a test split of ~1400 azimuth lines x ~2000 range samples yields on the order of 2 million curves; at 150 elevation bins that is ~1.2 GB per float32 array and ~2.4 GB per float64 copy, i.e. roughly 7 GB resident before any plotting. The image-AE path has the same shape (n_patches x C x H x W, kept twice in float32 and twice in float64).
suggested_fix: Accumulate the metric sums streaming over batches instead of concatenating the split, or at minimum compute the metrics in float32 / free the float32 result before upcasting, and keep only the subsampled patches needed by the plots.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. AeReconstructionPredictor.run_inference (pipelines/autoencoder_common/inference/predictor.py:37-56) concatenates every batch into three whole-split float32 arrays (gt, pred, embeddings), and AeMetricsBase.__init__ (pipelines/autoencoder_common/inference/metrics.py:13-17) immediately makes float64 copies of all three. Both sets stay resident: ProfileAeInferencePipeline.run holds `result` and `metrics_obj` at the same time (pipeline.py:104-109) and ProfileAePlots.compose consumes result.gt/result.pred/result.embeddings after the metrics object exists, so nothing can be freed. The claimed scale holds and is in fact understated: production defaults are dataset az1000-16000/rg500-4000 with test_azimuth=(14564,16000) over the full range extent, i.e. a test region of 1436 x 3500 = 5.0M pixels, pixel_subsample defaults to 1.0 (all active pixels + 5% of empties), and profile length = Layout.profile_length = tomogram.shape[0], which is 300 bins in the shipped preprocessing twin (600,000,128 B / 4 / (1000*500)), not 150. That is roughly 4.8 GB per float32 array and 9.6 GB per float64 copy at ~4M curves. Peak is higher still because _physical_errors builds diff plus several full-size float64 temporaries, _normalized_errors round-trips both arrays through float32 and back to float64, and _shape_errors/_power_errors take boolean-masked full copies. The inference scheduler runs one worker per GPU in config.gpus, so this peak multiplies across concurrent runs. No test pins the float64 upcast as intended behaviour (tests/ae_inference/test_metrics.py only checks values on tiny synthetic arrays), and this is not one of the listed known non-issues. It is not a hot-loop micro-inefficiency, but it is a concrete OOM/resource hazard on the path that every profile-AE and image-AE run takes at scoring time, so major is right.
correction: Line/location: the cited pipelines/profile_autoencoder/inference/pipeline.py:60 is only the call site; the actual mechanism is pipelines/autoencoder_common/inference/predictor.py:48-52 (three whole-split float32 concatenations) and pipelines/autoencoder_common/inference/metrics.py:14-16 (three float64 upcasts). Numbers: profile length is the tomogram bin count (300 in the shipped twin), not 150, and the default production test region is 1436 azimuth x 3500 range = ~5.0M pixels, not 1400x2000; so the float32 arrays are ~4.8 GB each and the float64 copies ~9.6 GB each. Mechanism is also incomplete: on top of the duplicated arrays, _physical_errors, _normalized_errors, _shape_errors and _power_errors each allocate further full-split float64 temporaries (diff, diff**2, np.abs(diff), the float32 round-trip in _normalized_errors, and the boolean-masked gt[self.active]/pred[self.active] copies), so the true peak is well above the ~7 GB quoted, and the inference scheduler fans out one such process per GPU in config.gpus.

title: UNETR silently slices the positional embedding instead of matching the token grid
description: `positional_embedding` is allocated for a `(image_size//patch_size)^2` grid, but the forward pass slices it to whatever token count the actual input produces. When the input is smaller than `config.image_size` (or non-square), the first N entries of a HxW grid do not correspond to the actual GhxGw grid, so every token gets a positional code from the wrong location — silently, with no error. Verified live: default `UNETRConfig` (image_size=256, patch_size=16, pos-emb 1x256x64) accepts a 1x1x64x64 input and runs, using positional codes 0..15 which are row 0 of a 16x16 grid rather than a 4x4 grid. `TransUNet` (models/backbone/trans_unet.py:120-130) handles the same situation correctly by interpolating the positional grid. The only thing preventing this in practice is the external guard `ModelBuilder.image_size_override`, which this slice quietly defeats; it also contradicts the project's "break loudly, no silent fallbacks" policy.
suggested_fix: Mirror TransUNet: reshape the positional embedding to the stored grid, `functional.interpolate` it to `(grid_height, grid_width)`, and flatten back — or raise when `tokens.shape[1] != self.positional_embedding.shape[1]`.
verdict_notes:
Reproduced from source and live.

Mechanism (models/backbone/unetr.py):
- Line 78 allocates `positional_embedding` with `(image_size // patch_size) ** 2` entries; `PatchEmbedding.forward` (models/blocks.py:614-619) returns tokens flattened row-major over the actual `(grid_height, grid_width)`, and `tokens_to_feature_map` reassembles row-major, so entry k of the parameter means grid cell (k // W_cfg, k % W_cfg) of the CONFIGURED grid.
- Line 197 `tokens + self.positional_embedding[:, :tokens.shape[1], :]` therefore hands token (i, j) of an actual Gh x Gw grid the code for configured-grid cell (n // W_cfg, n % W_cfg) with n = i*Gw + j. Whenever Gw != W_cfg the 2-D correspondence is wrong, with no error.

Live check (Dune env, UNETRConfig(image_size=256, patch_size=16, embedding_dim=64, transformer_layers=4, heads=4, decoder_features=[32,16,8,8])):
- pos-emb (1, 256, 64); a 1x1x64x64 input runs fine and returns (1, 6, 64, 64), consuming codes 0..15, i.e. row 0 of a 16x16 grid used as if it were a 4x4 grid.
- A 512x512 input raises RuntimeError ("size of tensor a (1024) must match tensor b (256)"), so the mismatch is loud in one direction and silent in the other — an asymmetry that is itself evidence this is unintended rather than designed.
- TransUNet (models/backbone/trans_unet.py:119-131) hits the identical situation and interpolates the positional grid, tracking `expected_grid_size`; UNETR neither interpolates nor validates.

Reachability. The auditor's framing of the guard is slightly off. `ModelBuilder.image_size_override` (pipelines/shared/model/model_builder.py:16-25, applied in backbone/dual/jepa training and inference loaders, benchmark sizing, batch_probe, dataloader tuning) forces image_size = square patch size and rejects rectangular patches, so mainline train/infer never mismatches (patching always pads to full patch size — pipelines/backbone/dataset/spatial.py:200 — so there are no short edge patches either). But the diagnostics probes are NOT covered by that guard: `ProbeWindows(run, self.config.window)` in receptive_field.py:167, input_attribution.py:186 and training_evolution.py:88 feed the loaded model windows of a config-chosen size (defaults 160, 64, 64 in configuration/diagnostics.py:207/249/366) independent of the run's patch size. Concrete failure: a UNETR run trained with a square patch of 128 (image_size=128, patch_size=16 -> 8x8 pos grid) probed by input_attribution/training_evolution with window=64 (4x4 grid) silently receives positional codes 0..15, which are rows 0-1 of the trained 8x8 grid, so every occlusion-attribution and evolution figure for that run is computed under positional codes the model never saw at those locations — wrong output, no warning.

Tests encode the matched case only: tests/models_backbone/_helpers.py sets `"unetr": {"image_size": WINDOW, ...}` with WINDOW=64, so the slice is a no-op there and the mismatch path is untested. This is a silent fallback of exactly the kind the project's "break loudly, no legacy/silent fallbacks" rule forbids, so it is not a known non-issue.
correction: Line and file are correct (models/backbone/unetr.py:197). Two refinements. (1) The claim that "the only thing preventing this in practice is the external guard ModelBuilder.image_size_override" is incomplete: that guard covers training/inference/benchmark model construction, but the diagnostics probe paths (pipelines/backbone/inference/receptive_field.py:167, input_attribution.py:186, training_evolution.py:88, via ProbeWindows) feed the model a config-chosen window size that is unrelated to the run's patch size, so the defect is reachable today for any UNETR run whose square patch is larger than the probe window. (2) The behaviour is asymmetric: an input LARGER than image_size fails loudly with a broadcast RuntimeError; only the smaller-input case is silent. Severity lowered from major to minor because no default/mainline path triggers it — the project's default patch (64, 32) is rectangular and is rejected outright for UNETR, so it needs a non-default square patch bigger than the diagnostic window to bite. Fix should mirror TransUNet: store expected_grid_size and either interpolate or raise on mismatch.

title: Tuple-valued 'categorical' choices break Optuna's RDB distribution round-trip
description: `DeepLabV3PlusConfig.atrous_rates` (line 726) and `U2NetLiteConfig.rsu_heights` (line 1181) declare sequence-valued choices under `"type": "categorical"`, which `ParamSampler.sample` forwards straight to `trial.suggest_categorical` (pipelines/tuning/tuners.py:25). Tuning uses SQLite RDB storage (`pipelines/tuning/pipeline.py:30`), which serialises the distribution to JSON; the tuples come back as lists, so the next trial's in-memory tuple-based distribution no longer compares equal to the stored one and Optuna's distribution-compatibility check rejects it. Every other sequence-valued parameter in this file (`features`, `depths`, `decoder_features`, `embedding_dims`, `block_layers`, `enc_blocks`, `cnn_features`) correctly uses the `indexed_categorical` form that exists precisely to avoid this.
suggested_fix: Change both entries to `"type": "indexed_categorical"` like the other sequence-valued parameters.
verdict_notes:
Reproduced from source and empirically.

Source chain verified:
- /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/configuration/architectures/backbone.py:726 `"atrous_rates": {"type": "categorical", "choices": [(1, 2, 4), (2, 4, 8), (1, 2, 4, 8)]}` and :1181 `"rsu_heights": {"type": "categorical", "choices": [(4, 3, 2), (5, 4, 3), (6, 5, 4)]}` — the only two sequence-valued entries in the file that are NOT `indexed_categorical` (features/depths/decoder_features/embedding_dims/block_layers/enc_blocks/cnn_features all use the indexed form).
- pipelines/tuning/tuners.py:25 `ParamSampler.sample` forwards `spec["choices"]` unchanged to `trial.suggest_categorical`; the space is `{**tunable_lr_params(), **tunable_arch_params()}` (Tuner.__init__), so the tuples reach Optuna verbatim.
- pipelines/tuning/pipeline.py:30 `self.storage_url = f"sqlite:///{self.run_dir / 'optuna.db'}"`, i.e. RDB (JSON-serialised) storage, and `_worker_job` spawns each worker as a **separate process** (`sys.executable entry_script --worker --storage-url ...`), `_dispatch_workers` runs one per GPU concurrently, and `--resume` reopens the same DB in new processes.
- `config_registry('backbone')` really contains `deeplabv3plus` and `u2net` (verified by importing it), so `_model_keys()` schedules them unless explicitly skipped.

Empirical reproduction (Dune env, optuna 4.8.0, sqlite storage):
- Process 1, fresh DB: works, but Optuna emits `UserWarning: Choices for a categorical distribution should be a tuple of None, bool, int, float and str for persistent storage but contains (1, 2, 4) which is of type tuple.` and the stored params come back as lists (`[2, 4, 8]`).
- Process 2 loading the same study and calling `suggest_categorical` with the same tuple choices: `ValueError: CategoricalDistribution does not support dynamic value space` raised from `optuna/storages/_rdb/storage.py:632 -> distributions.check_distribution_compatibility(previous_distribution, distribution)`; the trial is marked FAIL. The stored distribution deserialises to list-of-lists, which never equals the in-memory tuple-of-tuples.

Concrete failure: tuning `deeplabv3plus_*` or `u2net_*` with more than one GPU (the standard multi-worker fan-out) or with `--resume`, every trial in every worker process that did not write the parameter first raises and is recorded FAIL; those workers contribute zero completed trials, so `best_config.json` is built only from the single lucky worker (or "No completed trials" if none complete).
correction: Mechanism detail is slightly off: the failure is not "the next trial" in the same process. Optuna's per-process storage cache keeps the in-memory tuple distribution, so all trials inside the first worker process succeed. The ValueError hits the *first* `suggest_categorical` of any process whose cache is empty but whose DB already holds the param record — i.e. concurrent worker processes 1..N-1 in the per-GPU fan-out (`TuningScheduler._dispatch_workers`, pipelines/tuning/pipeline.py) and every worker in a `--resume` run; and because the distribution is never successfully cached there, every subsequent trial in that process fails too. Secondary effect even in the single-worker-single-process case: values round-trip through the DB as lists, so `BestConfigWriter` writes `"atrous_rates": [2, 4, 8]` rather than a tuple. Optuna also warns loudly at distribution construction, so the problem is visible in worker logs. Scope is limited to the two configs cited; fix is to switch both to `indexed_categorical` (or plain string choices).

title: snapshot_every_n_epochs is exposed in the launch form but never reaches the trainer
description: `TrainingQueueConfig.snapshot_every_n_epochs` is surfaced in the webui training-queue form (`webui/launch_layout.py:217`) and documented in `webui/config_descriptions.json`, but the only place that builds the trainer's `TrainingLoopConfig` is `ConfigFactory.training_trainer_config` (pipelines/shared/config/config_factory.py:92-103), and that constructor omits the field. Every training path (backbone launcher, dual, JEPA, benchmark, patch sweep, cross-validation, batch probe) goes through that factory, so `TrainingLoopConfig.snapshot_every_n_epochs` stays at its default 0 and `Trainer._maybe_snapshot` (tools/training/trainer.py:362-364) always returns early. Consequently no epoch snapshots are ever written and `main/analysis/animate_training.py` can only ever fail with "No epoch snapshots under .../checkpoints". No test covers the propagation.
suggested_fix: Add `snapshot_every_n_epochs = training.snapshot_every_n_epochs` to the `TrainingLoopConfig(...)` call in `ConfigFactory.training_trainer_config`, and add a test asserting the queue value reaches the trainer config.
verdict_notes:
I reproduced the whole chain from source.

1. `/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/configuration/training/general/run.py:49` defines `TrainingQueueConfig.snapshot_every_n_epochs: int = 0` (the entry-config field the launch form and ConfigCli write to).
2. `/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/webui/launch_layout.py:217` claims `"snapshot_every_n_epochs"` inside the `training_queue` "Schedule" group, and `webui/config_descriptions.json:1390,1423` documents it ("Save a weights-only epoch snapshot to checkpoints/epoch_<N>.pt every N epochs ... 0 disables"), so it is genuinely user-facing.
3. `/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/configuration/training/general/runtime.py:34` defines the runtime-side `TrainingLoopConfig.snapshot_every_n_epochs: int = 0`, which is what the trainer reads.
4. A repo-wide grep (all files, including tests/, main/, webui/static/js and JSON registries) for `snapshot_every_n_epochs` yields exactly seven hits: the two dataclass definitions, `trainer.py:364`, the error string in `pipelines/backbone/inference/training_evolution.py:57`, a docstring in `main/analysis/animate_training.py:17`, a purpose string in `webui/script_catalog.py:188`, the launch_layout claim, and the two config_descriptions entries. There is no assignment anywhere that copies queue -> loop config, and no test.
5. `grep -rn "TrainingLoopConfig("` shows the only production construction site is `pipelines/shared/config/config_factory.py:92-103`; the other four hits are AE tests. That constructor passes epochs, validation_frequency, use_amp, gradient_accumulation_steps, log_all_losses, log_debug, abort_on_nonfinite_loss, use_ema, ema_decay, resume — and omits snapshot_every_n_epochs.
6. Every training entry reaches that factory: `pipelines/backbone/training/launcher.py:57` (dual inherits this launcher), `pipelines/jepa/training/pipeline.py:34` (then `inherit_shared_from(base)`, which just copies the shared sub-configs including `training`), `pipelines/autoencoder_common/training.py:21`, `pipelines/benchmark/workers.py:152`, `pipelines/benchmark/batch_probe.py:49`, `pipelines/patch_sweep/workers.py:33`, `pipelines/cross_validation/workers.py:136`, `pipelines/tuning/workers.py:69`. None of them mutate `trainer_config.training.snapshot_every_n_epochs` afterwards (the launcher only sets `curriculum` and `geometry`; `pipelines/shared/training/overfit_check.py` only overrides epochs/validation_frequency/use_ema/resume).
7. Therefore `TrainingLoopConfig.snapshot_every_n_epochs` is always 0 at runtime, and `Trainer._maybe_snapshot` (tools/training/trainer.py:363-365, called each epoch at line 467) returns immediately on `every <= 0`. No `checkpoints/epoch_XXXX.pt` file is ever produced, so `pipelines/backbone/inference/training_evolution.py:55-59` always raises `FileNotFoundError("No epoch snapshots under .../checkpoints; train with snapshot_every_n_epochs > 0 ...")`, making `main/analysis/animate_training.py` unusable regardless of what the user sets in the form.

This is not one of the listed known non-issues: it is a silently ignored user-facing setting (the opposite of the project's "break loudly" policy), not a deliberate quirk.
correction: The claim is accurate; only the anchor is worth sharpening. The defect site is the omission in `ConfigFactory.training_trainer_config` at /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/pipelines/shared/config/config_factory.py:92-103 (the `TrainingLoopConfig(...)` call), with the corresponding runtime field at configuration/training/general/runtime.py:34; run.py:49 is merely where the exposed knob is declared. Fix: add `snapshot_every_n_epochs = training.snapshot_every_n_epochs` to that constructor. Note also that the setting is doubly dead-ended for the JEPA and autoencoder families, since they inherit the same `training` sub-config via `TrainerConfig.inherit_shared_from` (configuration/training/general/trainer.py:10-12).

title: A single NaN/Inf gradient silently defeats clipping and permanently poisons adaptive thresholds
description:
`maybe_clip` computes `norm = global_norm(model)`, which is NaN as soon as any parameter gradient contains NaN/Inf. Three things then fail silently, in sequence:

1. Line 112 `if norm > self.EXPLODING_NORM_SENTINEL` — `nan > 100.0` is False, so the exploding-gradient alert never fires (verified in the Dune env).
2. Line 75 `scale = min(1.0, max_norm / (norm + self.epsilon))` — `min(1.0, nan)` returns 1.0 in Python (verified), so the NaN gradients pass through **unscaled** into `optimizer.step()` and NaN the whole model. Clipping, the one mechanism meant to contain a gradient blow-up, becomes a no-op exactly when it is needed.
3. `record()` (line 143) appends the NaN into `self.history`. From then on `_compute_adaptive_threshold` returns NaN forever for both adaptive modes (`np.percentile([... nan ...], 95)` -> nan, `mean()+k*std()` -> nan, both verified), so `_clip` is called with `max_norm=nan` on every subsequent step and adaptive clipping is permanently disabled for the rest of the run. The NaN also survives `state_dict()`/`load_state_dict`, so it is carried across a resume.

On top of that, `check_gradients` (line 95) is the only code that would actually detect this, and (a) it runs only when `tracker.debug` is on and (b) its return value is discarded at line 108 — nothing acts on `has_invalid`.
evidence:
def _clip(self, model: torch.nn.Module, norm: float, max_norm: float) -> tuple[float, float]:
        scale = min(1.0, max_norm / (norm + self.epsilon))
suggested_fix: In `maybe_clip`, test `math.isfinite(norm)` right after `global_norm`. On a non-finite norm: log an error, zero the gradients (or raise when `abort_on_nonfinite_loss` is set), skip the optimizer step, and do **not** append the value to `self.history`. Also consume the `check_gradients` return value instead of discarding it, and filter non-finite entries in `_compute_adaptive_threshold`.
verdict_notes:
Mechanics reproduce from source (/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/tools/training/gradients.py, /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/tools/training/trainer.py:250-273):

- global_norm (line 49-58) returns nan for a grad tensor containing nan (verified with torch in the Dune env: norm nan case -> nan, inf case -> inf).
- Line 112 `nan > 100.0` is False -> the exploding-norm alert is skipped (verified).
- Line 75 `min(1.0, nan)` returns 1.0 in CPython (min keeps the running minimum since `nan < 1.0` is False) -> scale 1.0 (verified).
- record() (line 143) appends nan; _compute_adaptive_threshold on a window containing nan returns nan for both branches (np.percentile -> nan, mean()+k*std() -> nan, verified with numpy). state_dict/load_state_dict (148-153) round-trip the nan.
- check_gradients is gated on tracker.debug (line 107) and its bool return is discarded (line 108); no other finite check on parameters or grads exists anywhere in tools/training or pipelines (grep for isfinite/isnan) — the only guard is `torch.isfinite(loss)` at trainer.py:250/321.

So the described code paths are real. What I dispute is the impact framing, which inflates this well past what actually happens.

1. "Clipping becomes a no-op exactly when it is needed" is misleading. _clip only rescales; nan * any_scale == nan, so no value of `scale` could ever have contained a NaN gradient. Getting scale=1.0 instead of some other number changes nothing for the NaN parameter itself. The only real loss is that other, finite-but-large grads in the same step also escape scaling.

2. The auditor missed the one case on line 75 where clipping genuinely does damage: with a true +inf grad, norm=inf, so scale = min(1.0, max_norm/(inf+eps)) = 0.0 and `p.grad.mul_(0.0)` turns inf into nan (IEEE inf*0 = nan, verified) — clipping manufactures NaN out of an exploding gradient. Relatedly, merely huge-but-finite grads whose sum of squares overflows to inf get multiplied by exactly 0, silently discarding the entire update. Both are the same line and are a stronger argument than the one made.

3. "Permanently disables adaptive clipping for the rest of the run" and "carried across a resume" are close to unreachable in practice. The default clip_mode is "fixed" (configuration/training/general/optimization.py:67, configuration/training/general/run.py:67), where history is used only for the TensorBoard histogram and a nan there has zero effect on clipping. Even under a non-default adaptive mode, a nan grad norm means the very next optimizer.step() NaNs the parameters, so the next batch's loss is non-finite and trainer.py:259 raises FloatingPointError (abort_on_nonfinite_loss defaults to True in both run.py:45 and runtime.py:30) — the run dies loudly, which is the project's stated preference. With abort disabled, every subsequent loss is non-finite, so `loss.backward()` never runs, `window_has_grads` stays False, and maybe_clip is never called again — there is no "rest of the run" during which the poisoned threshold does anything.

4. The debug gating of check_gradients is deliberate, not an oversight: the constructor prints "NaN grad scan: on (log_debug) / off (enable with training.log_debug)" (line 43), i.e. it is advertised as an opt-in diagnostic scan, and its contract is to warn via the logger.

Net: a real robustness gap in _clip and in the nan-vs-sentinel comparison, worth fixing (guard `math.isfinite(norm)` before clipping/recording, and act on check_gradients), but not a major silent-corruption bug — the default configuration turns this into a loud abort one batch later.
correction: Line and file are right (tools/training/gradients.py:75, with lines 112 and 143 also implicated). Corrections to the mechanism: (a) no `scale` value could contain a NaN gradient — `nan * scale == nan` — so "clipping becomes a no-op exactly when needed" overstates part 2; the genuine defect on that line is the inf case, where scale = min(1.0, max_norm/(inf+eps)) = 0.0 and `p.grad.mul_(0.0)` converts inf into NaN, and the overflow case, where huge-but-finite grads whose norm overflows to inf are multiplied by 0 and the whole update is silently discarded; (b) the permanent adaptive-threshold poisoning requires a non-default clip_mode (default is "fixed", where history never feeds clipping) and is effectively unreachable because a NaN grad norm NaNs the parameters on the same step, after which trainer.py:259 raises FloatingPointError by default (abort_on_nonfinite_loss=True) or, with abort disabled, every later batch is skipped so maybe_clip is never called again; (c) the debug gating of check_gradients is deliberate and advertised in the startup table ("NaN grad scan: on (log_debug)"), so only the discarded return value is a fair criticism. Suggested fix: in maybe_clip, test `math.isfinite(norm)` before the sentinel comparison, before calling _clip, and before record(), and raise (or skip the step) on a non-finite norm rather than scaling.

title: Checkpoint and resume-state writes are not atomic; a kill mid-write destroys the run
description:
`TrainerState.save` (line 169) rewrites `last.pt` in place at the end of every epoch, and `Checkpoint.save` (line 50) rewrites `best_model.pt` in place on every improvement. Both use a bare `torch.save` straight onto the destination path. If the process dies between the truncate and the final flush — which this project actively expects: webui kill-job, GPU charity mode reclaiming a device, intrusion-driven eviction, OOM-killer — the file is left truncated.

The consequence for `last.pt` is total: `TrainerState.restore` is the only resume path, it hard-fails on a corrupt file, and there is no second copy, so the entire training run must be redone from epoch 0. For `best_model.pt` the run finishes but `restore_best` then fails to load and the reported test metrics are lost.

The repo already has the atomic-write pattern for the JSON side (`tools/data/io.py:20-31`, `FileIO.save_json(..., atomic=True)` writing `.tmp` then `os.replace`); it was simply never mirrored for the torch payloads, which are the ones that actually take seconds to write and matter most.
suggested_fix: Write to `path.with_suffix('.pt.tmp')` and `os.replace(tmp, path)` after `torch.save` returns, in both `TrainerState.save` and `Checkpoint.save` — mirroring `FileIO.save_json(atomic=True)`. `os.replace` is atomic within a filesystem, so a kill at any point leaves either the previous good file or the new one.
verdict_notes:
I reproduced the claim from source and could not refute it.

1. The cited code is exactly as quoted. `/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/tools/training/checkpoint.py:169` is `torch.save(TrainerState.capture(...), str(path))` writing straight onto the destination, and `checkpoint.py:50` is `torch.save(checkpoint, path)` after `os.makedirs`. No `.tmp` + `os.replace`, no fsync, no backup copy. `torch.save` to a path opens the destination with mode `wb` (truncating it) and then streams the zip payload, so death mid-write leaves a truncated, unloadable file — not the previous good one.

2. The write really is per-epoch on the hot path: `tools/training/trainer.py:466` calls `TrainerState.save(self, epoch, self.state_path, loader_generator)` unconditionally at the end of every epoch, and `Checkpoint.step` (checkpoint.py:35) calls `save` on every val improvement. Payload is model + optimizer + EMA shadow + RNG states, i.e. seconds of I/O, so the vulnerable window is not negligible.

3. There is no second copy to fall back to. Grepping the whole repo for `last.pt` yields only `checkpoint.py:120` (the constant) and `pipelines/shared/training/overfit_check.py:146` (a cleanup list). `TrainerState.restore` (checkpoint.py:172-195) is the sole resume reader, reached only from `Trainer._maybe_resume` (trainer.py:376-390), and it hard-fails on a bad file. `best_model.pt` cannot substitute: `Trainer.capture_state` (trainer.py:211-216) stores only `{epoch, params, x_axis}` — no optimizer, scheduler, early-stopping or RNG state — so a lost `last.pt` genuinely means restarting from epoch 0.

4. The kill scenarios are real in this repo, not hypothetical. `webui/process_manager.py:719/733` sends SIGTERM to the process group and SIGKILL after an 8 s grace; `stop_all`/NUKE at 845-856 does the same; `webui/resource_watchdog.py:84 _check_kill` kills on RAM pressure. `tools/orchestration/gpu_queue.py:220-236` terminates then `.kill()`s workers past `terminate_deadline_s`, and its own log line literally says "terminated N workers, resume with --resume" — resume-after-signal is a designed workflow, and the artifact that workflow depends on is written non-atomically. Training workers install no SIGTERM handler, so default disposition is immediate death mid-`torch.save`; SIGKILL is uncatchable regardless.

5. The comparison to existing practice holds: `tools/data/io.py:20-31` implements `save_json(..., atomic=True)` via `.tmp` + `os.replace`, and it is actively used at `tools/orchestration/gpu_queue.py:50,191` and `pipelines/tuning/tuners.py:68`. The pattern exists and was simply never applied to the torch payloads.

6. No test encodes the current behaviour as intended — `tests/training_runtime/test_trainer_state.py` only round-trips save/restore, and grepping tests for atomic/truncat/corrupt/partial returns nothing. This is not one of the listed known non-issues (it is not a legacy-fallback matter; adding an atomic rename does not shim any old artifact).

The only thing that keeps this from being "critical" is that it needs a kill inside the write window rather than firing deterministically; the blast radius when it does fire is a whole training run.
correction:
Line numbers and mechanism are correct. Two refinements to the stated impact:

(a) The `best_model.pt` consequence is understated. It is not only `restore_best` that suffers — `best_model.pt` is the handoff artifact for the entire downstream stack: `pipelines/jepa/training/pipeline.py:49,58,244` loads the profile/image autoencoder `best_model.pt`, `pipelines/shared/comparison/trial_collection.py:122` and `pipelines/patch_sweep/report.py:66` rglob for it, and `tools/training/trainer.py:37` defines it as the run's checkpoint path. A truncated `best_model.pt` therefore breaks inference, comparison, patch-sweep reporting and JEPA training that depend on that run, not just the final test metrics.

(b) The same non-atomic pattern exists in two more places the claim does not mention and which a fix should cover: `tools/training/trainer.py:372` (`_maybe_snapshot`, per-N-epoch `epoch_XXXX.pt`) and `pipelines/unrolled/training/trainer.py:159`. These are lower stakes than `last.pt` but are the same defect.

Severity stays major.

title: Interpreter path is taken verbatim from the request body and executed, with no allow-list
description: `/api/run`, `/api/saved-runs` and `/api/tensorboard/start` accept an arbitrary `interpreter` string from the POST body and hand it straight to `subprocess.Popen` (`process_manager.py:190` builds `argv = [record["interpreter"], "-u", script, ...]`; `tensorboard_manager.py:74` builds `[interpreter, "-m", "tensorboard.main"]`). Every other launch input is validated — the script key against `ProjectPaths.SCRIPT_DIRS` (`request_router.py:563`), override names against `OVERRIDE_NAME` (`process_manager.py:299`) — but the executable itself is not checked against `ProjectPaths.discover_interpreters()`. Combined with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every JSON response (`request_router.py:917`) and `_read_json` ignoring Content-Type (`request_router.py:892`), any web page the user visits can issue a non-preflighted `text/plain` POST to `127.0.0.1:8765/api/run` and cause an arbitrary binary to be executed as the user. This is an asymmetry in the validation the code already performs, not a hypothetical: the script whitelist is deliberately enforced while the interpreter is not.
evidence:
interpreter = body.get("interpreter") or self._preferred_interpreter(key)
result      = self._execute_run(key, interpreter, body.get("overrides", {}), ...)
suggested_fix: Validate the requested interpreter against the set returned by `ProjectPaths.discover_interpreters()` (reject anything not in it) before passing it to ProcessManager/TensorboardManager, and drop the wildcard CORS header on state-changing endpoints.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. request_router.py:566 does `interpreter = body.get("interpreter") or self._preferred_interpreter(key)` and passes it unvalidated to `_execute_run` -> ProcessManager.launch/enqueue -> `_start`, where process_manager.py:190 builds `argv = [record["interpreter"], "-u", str(entry["path"]), *entry["args"]]` and Popen executes it (process_manager.py:181 also derives LD_LIBRARY_PATH from the same string). No code path validates the interpreter: SavedRunStore.save (saved_run_store.py:28-30) only rejects an empty string, and ProjectPaths has no interpreter check at all. The allow-list the claim points at does exist and is unused for validation: ProjectPaths.discover_interpreters() (project_paths.py:145) is only used to populate the UI dropdown (request_router.py:839, web_ui_server.py:172, script_catalog.py:325). Meanwhile has_script (project_paths.py:128) gates the script key and OVERRIDE_NAME (process_manager.py:60,299) gates override names, so the asymmetry the auditor describes is factual. There is no auth, no Origin/Referer/Host check in web_ui_server.py or request_router.py, and _read_json (request_router.py:891) ignores Content-Type, so a cross-site simple POST (text/plain) to 127.0.0.1:8765/api/run is accepted. The frontend only ever sends interpreter values chosen from the discovered list (launch.js:606-607/862/883, ablation.js:130, console.js:391-392), so validating against discover_interpreters() would break nothing. Not one of the listed known non-issues. Severity major is appropriate: the server binds 127.0.0.1 by default and is already an unauthenticated launcher for ~50 repo scripts, which caps the marginal risk, but argv[0] control plus the `-c` sink is a genuine escalation over "run an allow-listed repo script".
correction: Three details to adjust. (1) A third, stronger sink is missing from the claim: webui/script_config_resolver.py:133 runs `argv = [interpreter, "-c", self.BOOTSTRAP, ...]` via subprocess.run, reachable from POST /api/tensorboard/start (request_router.py:734-735 -> _training_logdir -> resolver.resolve(key, interpreter)); that is argv[0] plus `-c`, a cleaner execution primitive than the process_manager path. (2) The tensorboard_manager.py:74 sink is only a fallback -- line 73 does `tb_bin = shutil.which("tensorboard")` and the `[interpreter, "-m", "tensorboard.main"]` form is used only when tensorboard is absent from PATH. (3) The CORS reasoning is slightly wrong: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` is not what permits the cross-origin write; a text/plain POST is a CORS "simple request" and is delivered (and executed) with or without that header. The wildcard header only additionally lets the attacking page read the JSON response (job ids, discovered interpreter paths). Also note the practical ceiling on the process_manager path: argv[1] is fixed to "-u" and the remaining args are the allow-listed script path plus `--<name> <value>` pairs, so the attacker picks an arbitrary executable but with partly constrained arguments. Fix is one line: reject any interpreter not present in ProjectPaths.discover_interpreters(), which breaks no legitimate UI flow.

title: Job records and their output buffers are never pruned, so the console grows without bound
description: `self.jobs` and `self.streams` are only ever added to — `launch`, `enqueue`, `_schedule` and `_adopt_orphan` insert, and the only removal is the rollback in `launch()` when `_start` fails. Every job keeps a `JobStream` whose `buffer` is a `deque(maxlen=4000)` of stdout chunks of up to 4096 bytes each, i.e. up to ~16 MB of retained text per job. Adopted orphans (`_adopt_orphan`, line 522) add a new record for every untracked `main/` process the `/api/jobs` poll ever sees, so a console left running for days over a training campaign accumulates hundreds of records and their buffers. `list_jobs()` also re-serialises the whole set on every poll, and `_advance_queue`'s `busy` scan walks all of them.
suggested_fix: Cap retained history: evict finished/failed/cancelled records (and their JobStreams) beyond a bounded recent count or age, and drop the stream buffer once a job has ended and no subscriber remains.
verdict_notes:
Reproduced from source in /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/webui/process_manager.py.

Insertions into `self.jobs`/`self.streams`: `launch` (95-96), `enqueue` (132-133), `_schedule` (234-235), `_adopt_orphan` (546-547). The only deletion in the whole file is the rollback at 101-102 when `_start` returns an error. Grepping the rest of webui/ for `streams`/`prune`/`MAX_JOBS`/`cleanup` finds nothing — no eviction, no cap, no TTL, and `tests/webui/test_process_manager_*.py` contain no retention test. Terminal states (`finished`, `failed`, `cancelled`) only mutate `record["status"]` (348, 264, 399, 697); the record and its `JobStream` stay in the dicts for the lifetime of the server process, which is explicitly designed to be long-lived (ServerDetacher retroactively nohups the server, and the home page polls `/api/jobs` every 5 s at webui/static/js/home.js:158).

Retained bytes per launched job are real: `_pump` (313-336) reads `os.read(fd, 4096)` and publishes one `{"type":"chunk","data":text}` event per read into `JobStream.buffer = deque(maxlen=4000)` (line 31). A high-throughput training log fills the ring with near-4096-byte chunks, i.e. roughly 16 MB retained per job, held forever after the job exits. Nothing frees it.

So the core claim — unbounded growth of `self.jobs`/`self.streams` — is confirmed. Two of the auditor's supporting details do not survive checking, and one cost estimate is wrong (see correction).
correction:
Mechanism corrections:

1. Adopted orphans do NOT carry the ~16 MB buffers. `_adopt_orphan` (522) publishes exactly one status event and starts `_watch_detached`, which never reads stdout (adopted tiles have no output by design); its stream holds 3 events total, so an orphan record costs ~1 KB, not megabytes. The multi-MB retention applies only to jobs launched by the console through `_pump`.

2. "add a new record for every untracked main/ process the poll ever sees" overstates it. `_orphan_candidates` skips any pid already mapped to a running record via `job_for_pid` (455) and drops candidates that are descendants of another candidate (460); `adopt_orphans` is also throttled to one scan per 3 s (419). `tests/webui/test_process_manager_orphans.py::test_tracked_job_is_not_readopted` and `::test_child_of_matching_process_is_not_adopted_twice` encode this. Adoption therefore adds one record per distinct top-level untracked process, not per poll, and GPU fan-out children of a tracked parent are not adopted.

3. The per-poll CPU costs named in the claim are negligible and should not be part of the finding: `list_jobs` does N shallow dict copies plus a sort of a few hundred small dicts, and `_advance_queue`'s `busy` scan is a dict-values pass. The only per-poll I/O that scales is `progress()` (a file read per *running* job), which is bounded by concurrent jobs, not by accumulated history. The actual defect is retained RSS proportional to the number of console-launched jobs (~ up to 16 MB each), plus an ever-growing job list rendered in the UI (console.js `_renderList` iterates every record, finished ones included).

Correct anchor is the whole insert/never-delete pattern (lines 95-96, 132-133, 234-235, 546-547) rather than just the declarations at 72-73.

Severity: this is a slow leak in a developer-facing research console, bounded per job and cleared by restarting the server, with no correctness impact — minor, not major.

title: Adopting an orphan runs a config-resolution subprocess inside the /api/jobs HTTP handler
description: `GET /api/jobs` calls `self.processes.adopt_orphans()` synchronously (`request_router.py:508`). For each newly seen orphan, `_adopt_orphan` calls `JobDescriber.describe(...)`, which calls `ScriptConfigResolver.resolve(...)`, which spawns `python -c BOOTSTRAP` with `timeout=180` (`script_config_resolver.py:136`). That bootstrap imports `tools.runtime.config_cli`, which transitively imports `tools.reporting` and matplotlib, so it costs seconds per (script, interpreter) pair not yet cached — and the orphan's interpreter is whatever `argv[0]` the terminal used, which may not match any cached entry. The UI's job-poll request therefore blocks on one or more heavyweight subprocesses; in the worst case (an interpreter that hangs on import) it blocks for the full 180 s timeout per orphan. The adoption tests all use a `StubDescriber`, so this path is untested.
suggested_fix: Adopt with an empty description and fill it in from a background thread, or move `adopt_orphans()` off the request path into the existing watcher thread.
verdict_notes:
The code chain the auditor describes is real, and I traced every hop:

- `/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/webui/request_router.py:508` — `GET /api/jobs` calls `self.processes.adopt_orphans()` synchronously before `list_jobs()`.
- `webui/process_manager.py:416-426` — `adopt_orphans` is throttled by `ORPHAN_RESCAN_S = 3.0` (line 63), scans `/proc`, and calls `_adopt_orphan` per candidate.
- `webui/process_manager.py:528` — the record dict builds `"description": self.describer.describe(info["script"], info["interpreter"], overrides)`, i.e. inside the request thread, before the record is inserted under the lock.
- `webui/job_describer.py:373-247` — `describe` -> `_values` -> `self.resolver.resolve(key, interpreter)`.
- `webui/script_config_resolver.py:150-171` — cache key is `(key, interpreter)`; on a miss `_run_bootstrap` does `subprocess.run([interpreter, "-c", BOOTSTRAP, ...], timeout=180)`.
- `webui/process_manager.py:458` — `"interpreter": tokens[0]` is the orphan's raw `argv[0]`, so for a terminal launch (`python main/training/train_backbone.py`) the key is `("train_backbone", "python")`, which will not match the `/api/scripts/<k>/config` cache entries keyed by the absolute `_preferred_interpreter` path. The auditor's cache-miss argument holds.
- `tests/webui/test_process_manager_orphans.py:32,43` — the only adoption tests inject a `StubDescriber`, and `adopt_orphans` has no other caller in the repo, so the real describe path is indeed untested.

I measured the bootstrap for `configuration.training.backbone` / `BackboneEntryConfig` with the Dune interpreter: 1.38 s wall. So the blocking is real but modest.

Where the claim overstates things:
1. The import cost attribution is wrong. The bootstrap stubs the `tools` package (`types.ModuleType('tools')`), so `tools/__init__.py` never runs, and `tools/runtime/__init__.py` is lazy (`__getattr__` + `importlib`). Importing `tools.runtime.config_cli` costs 11 ms and pulls in only argparse/ast/`detacher`. `matplotlib` is never imported (`'matplotlib' in sys.modules` is False). The ~1.0 s comes from `__import__(configuration.training.backbone)` dragging in torch.
2. The cost is not per-request. `_orphan_candidates` skips any pid whose `job_for_pid` resolves (line 455), and an adopted record is immediately `status == "running"`, so a given orphan triggers exactly one `describe`. The 5 s `/api/jobs` poll (`static/js/console.js:365`, `home.js:158`) therefore pays nothing in steady state; the subprocess is a cold path sitting inside a hot handler.
3. The server is `ThreadingHTTPServer` (`webui/web_ui_server.py:4,43`), so the 1.4 s delay hits only the one polling request, not the whole console. Concurrent polls short-circuit on the 3 s throttle.
4. The 180 s worst case is speculative. If `argv[0]` is a bare `python` not on the server's PATH, `subprocess.run` raises `FileNotFoundError` immediately and `_run_bootstrap` returns `{"ok": False}`; `_values` then silently degrades to overrides-only text. No hang, and no failure caching — but the retry is still once per new orphan.

So: real synchronous subprocess in an HTTP handler, worth moving off the request thread, but it is a one-time ~1.4 s delay per newly detected orphan on a threaded server, not the repeated multi-second stall the claim implies.
correction: Mechanism is correct but the cost model is off in two ways. (a) The expensive import is the *configuration* module (torch, ~1.0 s), not `tools.reporting`/matplotlib — the bootstrap replaces `tools` with a stub `ModuleType` so `tools/__init__.py` never executes, and `tools/runtime/__init__.py` resolves lazily; `tools.runtime.config_cli` itself costs 11 ms and matplotlib is never loaded. Total measured subprocess: 1.38 s. (b) It is not a recurring per-request cost: `_orphan_candidates` (process_manager.py:455) skips pids already backed by a running job, so `describe` runs exactly once per orphan process, and `ThreadingHTTPServer` (web_ui_server.py:43) confines the stall to the single polling request. The 180 s worst case is not reachable through the realistic failure mode (a bare `python` argv[0] missing from PATH raises OSError instantly and degrades to an overrides-only description). Severity is minor: worth deferring the describe to a background thread and keying the resolver cache on a resolved interpreter path, not a blocking defect. Line 528 and the untested-path observation (StubDescriber in tests/webui/test_process_manager_orphans.py:32) are accurate.

title: A phase transition that cannot be applied is recorded as applied, so a deferred pool SHRINK is silently converted into "keep everything"
description: `tick()` writes the new phase into `self.applied[job_id]` (line 270) before `_cross` runs, and `_cross` records `withheld` and returns early when no GPU of the target pool is grantable. The only recovery path is `sweep()`, and `_claim` (line 374) computes `sorted(set(current) | set(freed))` — a union, i.e. it can only GROW a pool. For a growing transition (weekday -> night/weekend) that is correct. For a shrinking transition it is wrong: weekend pool [0,1,2,3] -> weekday pool [2,3] with 2 and 3 held by a colleague yields granted=[], the job keeps [0,1,2,3], and the phase is already latched as "weekday" so `tick` never retries. When 2 and 3 later free, `sweep` computes merged == sorted(current) so nothing is written, yet line 410 still drains `record["withheld"]`. The job therefore holds the full night pool through the whole workday, which is precisely what the weekday schedule exists to prevent. The same latching means any `set_gpus` failure at line 249 permanently loses that transition. Tests only cover the growing direction (tests/webui/test_gpu_schedule.py::test_a_pool_held_entirely_by_others_leaves_the_job_untouched).
suggested_fix: Only latch `applied[job_id]["phase"]` after `_cross` reports success, so the next tick retries the crossing; and have `sweep` re-derive the pool from `gpus_for(record["phase"])` intersected with availability instead of unioning `current` with `freed`, so a deferred shrink is still a shrink.
verdict_notes:
I reproduced the exact failure from source with a standalone test driving the real `GpuSchedule` against the repo's own stubs (/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/tests/webui/test_gpu_schedule.py fixtures).

Mechanism, traced in /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/webui/gpu_schedule.py:
- `tick` (line 268-275) latches the new phase into `self.applied[job_id]` at line 270 BEFORE calling `_cross`, and line 272 skips any job whose recorded phase already equals the current phase. So a transition that `_cross` could not carry out is never retried by `tick` until the NEXT phase boundary.
- `_cross` (236-246) computes `granted = availability.grant(target)` minus gifts; when every GPU of the target pool is held by another user, `granted == []`, it logs "left job ... where it is" and returns without calling `set_gpus`. `withheld` is set to the full target.
- The only deferred-recovery path is `sweep` -> `_claim` (373-383), which computes `merged = sorted(set(current) | set(freed))` — a pure union. For a growing transition (weekday [2,3] -> night/weekend [0,1,2,3]) the union is right. For a shrinking transition it is a no-op: `merged == sorted(current)` -> return [] at line 376, and yet line 410 unconditionally drains `record["withheld"]` of the freed GPUs, so the pending transition is discarded.

Concrete run (real class, stub processes/system): job live on [0,1,2,3] during the weekend, GPUs 2 and 3 occupied by "colleague", `tick(Monday 09:00)` (phase weekday, target [2,3]):
  after transition: writes=[] pool=[0,1,2,3] applied={'job1': {'phase': 'weekday', 'withheld': [2,3]}}
  after 2,3 free + sweep: writes=[] pool=[0,1,2,3] applied={'job1': {'phase': 'weekday', 'withheld': []}}
  later weekday tick+sweep: writes=[] pool=[0,1,2,3]
The job holds the full night/weekend pool for the whole workday, i.e. it keeps GPUs 0 and 1 that the weekday pool exists to hand back to colleagues, and no log line reports the lost shrink after the initial warning.

The existing tests only encode the growing direction: `test_a_pool_held_entirely_by_others_leaves_the_job_untouched` (line 250) runs weekday->night, and every greedy/sweep test (263-344) starts from a grow. The 49 existing tests still pass; my shrink test is the only failure.

I also confirmed the secondary claim: at line 249, a `set_gpus` failure returns early while the phase stays latched. When the pool was fully grantable, `withheld` is empty, so `sweep` skips the job at line 398 and the transition is lost until the next phase boundary. `ProcessManager.set_gpus` (webui/process_manager.py:656-680) does return `{"ok": False}` for real transient states ("job is not running", pool file not yet present), so this path is reachable, though rarer.

Ruled out alternatives: nothing outside gpu_schedule.py touches `self.applied` (grep over webui/*.py shows only ProcessManager's unrelated `applied` Event); `update()` does not reset the latch; `_watch` calls `tick` every 30 s and `sweep` every 600 s, so there is no other retry. This is not one of the listed deliberate GPU-orchestration designs (those cover intrusion order, charity naps, VRAM reservation), and the "leave it where it is" warning is a same-tick fallback, not a documented decision to abandon the transition permanently.
correction: The latch is at line 270 (`tick`), not 244; line 244-246 is the early return in `_cross` that triggers it. Two scope corrections to the auditor's write-up: (1) the loss is not limited to greedy mode — with `greedy` off or during a charity nap, `sweep` returns at line 391 and the blocked shrink is equally unrecoverable, so greedy is not the safety net; (2) besides the fully-blocked case, if `set_gpus` fails at 248 while `withheld` is non-empty, a later `sweep` will `_claim` the union of the stale current pool and the freed target GPUs, producing a pool that matches no phase. The trigger window is narrow (every GPU of the target pool must be occupied by another user at the exact 30 s tick of the transition), so "major" is at the upper end; the harm is GPU etiquette on a shared machine rather than incorrect results.

title: SystemHistory/ActiveUsers/du sample loops have no exception guard, and the GPU memory percentage is unguarded against a None field
description: `SystemHistory.sample` guards `device["util"]` against None on line 402 (nvidia-smi prints `[N/A]`, which `_num` maps to None) but then divides with `device["mem_used"]` unguarded on line 403. A None there raises TypeError. All three background loops started in `__init__` (lines 35-37) — `_du_loop` (268), `SystemHistory.sample_loop` (417), `ActiveUsers.sample_loop` (540) — are bare `while True: work(); sleep()` with no try/except, unlike every other monitor in the webui (gpu_watchdog.py:86, gpu_schedule.py:430, resource_watchdog.py:52, contention_monitor.py:110 all wrap the body). So a single transient nvidia-smi oddity permanently kills the thread and `/api/system` keeps serving a frozen `history`/`users` payload with no error anywhere — the home page graphs simply stop moving and nothing says why. `ActiveUsers._rows` has the same exposure via `sorted(held["gpus"])` when `device["index"]` is None.
evidence: mpct  = round(100.0 * device["mem_used"] / device["mem_total"], 1) if device["mem_total"] else 0.0
suggested_fix: Guard `mem_used` the same way `util` is guarded, and wrap the bodies of `_du_loop`, `SystemHistory.sample_loop` and `ActiveUsers.sample_loop` in try/except that logs through WebLogger, matching the other monitors.
verdict_notes:
Reproduced from source at /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/webui/system_monitor.py.

1. `_num` (line 335-340) does `float(raw)` in a try/except ValueError returning None, so nvidia-smi's `[N/A]` / `[Not Supported]` / `[Unknown Error]` cells become None for every numeric field of `_gpu_devices` (lines 152-162), including `mem_used`.

2. `SystemHistory.sample` line 402 explicitly guards `device["util"] is not None`, but line 403 is `mpct = round(100.0 * device["mem_used"] / device["mem_total"], 1) if device["mem_total"] else 0.0` — the guard is on `mem_total` only. A device row with `mem_used = [N/A]` and a valid `mem_total` (e.g. a card in an error/vGPU/MIG state) yields `100.0 * None / 40960` -> TypeError. The asymmetry is real: the author guarded util for exactly this N/A reason, and tests/webui/test_system_history.py:16-19 encodes both known N/A shapes (util None, mem_total 0) but not mem_used None.

3. No exception guard anywhere on the path: `sample_loop` (417-420), `ActiveUsers.sample_loop` (540-543) and `_du_loop` (268-272) are bare `while True: work(); sleep()`. The four sibling monitors all wrap their body and log: gpu_watchdog.py `_watch` (`except Exception as exc: self.logger.error(f"gpu watchdog error: ...")`), gpu_schedule.py:420-432, resource_watchdog.py:46-53, contention_monitor.py:102-111. `SystemMonitor` has no logger at all, and no `threading.excepthook` is installed anywhere in webui/ or main/.

4. Consequence is concrete: the daemon thread exits, `SystemHistory.state()` / `ActiveUsers.state()` keep returning the last-filled ring buffers, and `/api/system` (snapshot lines 342-361) keeps serving a frozen `history`/`users` payload. Nothing restarts or health-checks the threads (no `is_alive` anywhere). The JS mirror of the same expression, webui/static/js/home.js:628, is safe only because JS coerces null to 0.
correction: Two details are overstated. (a) "a single transient nvidia-smi oddity" is too broad: `_gpu_devices`, `_compute_apps`, `_memory`, `_cpu_counters`, `_du`, `_sessions` and `ProcStats.*` all already swallow OSError/TimeoutExpired/ValueError, and util/mem_total N/A are guarded — the one reproducible crash input is `mem_used = [N/A]` (or ERR!/Unknown Error) together with a numeric `mem_total`. (b) The `ActiveUsers._rows` `sorted(held["gpus"])` exposure is weaker than stated: a set containing only `None` sorts fine (no comparison happens), so it needs at least two devices with one N/A `index`, which nvidia-smi effectively never emits. Also, the thread death is not literally silent — Python's default threading excepthook prints the traceback to the server's stderr; what is missing is any Logger line, any UI signal, and any recovery, so the operator-visible symptom is exactly as described (graphs stop moving, nothing in the console UI explains it). Severity is monitoring-surface only (no effect on training, inference or results) with an uncommon trigger, so minor rather than major; the right fix is the sibling-monitor pattern (try/except + logger.error in the three loops) plus a None guard on `mem_used`.

title: smaps_rollup is read for every process on the machine every 2 s (and again every 5 s), a page-table walk per process
description: `ProcStats.attributed` reads `/proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup`, which forces the kernel to walk the whole address space of the target process. `ActiveUsers._scan` calls it for EVERY pid on the box (not just the current user's) on a 2 s loop, and `ContentionMonitor._scan` (contention_monitor.py:270) does the same on a 5 s loop. On this machine that means several hundred full address-space walks per second of wall clock, including multi-hundred-GB training processes where a single rollup read costs tens of milliseconds. There is no caching, no throttling and no sharing between the two scanners. The irony is that ContentionMonitor exists to detect the user slowing down neighbours while itself being a continuous system-wide load. Note the PSS attribution itself is a deliberate design decision (per the project notes); the defect is the rate and the duplication, not the metric.
suggested_fix: Share one /proc walk between ActiveUsers and ContentionMonitor, and refresh the expensive PSS value on a slower cadence (e.g. every Nth sample, or only for pids above an RSS floor) while keeping the cheap statm-based figure between refreshes.
verdict_notes:
Reproduced from source and measured on this machine.

Mechanism, traced:
- webui/proc_stats.py:39 `ProcStats.attributed` -> :19 `ProcStats.pss` opens and reads `/proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup` (full VMA/page-table walk in the kernel, no caching anywhere in the class).
- webui/system_monitor.py:464 `ActiveUsers._scan` iterates every entry in `/proc` and calls `ProcStats.attributed(pid)` for each; `sample_loop` (line 540-543) runs it forever with `SAMPLE_PERIOD_S = 2.0`. The thread is started unconditionally in `SystemMonitor.__init__` (line 37).
- webui/contention_monitor.py:270 `ContentionMonitor._scan` does the identical per-pid `attributed()` call inside `_watch`'s `INTERVAL = 5.0` loop; `ContentionMonitor.start()` is called unconditionally by web_ui_server.py:150.
- No cache, no throttle, no sharing between the two scanners: both walk `/proc` independently and neither memoizes.

Measured on this box (150 own pids, desktop-sized processes): one full pass costs 137 ms of pure `smaps_rollup` time, with a single 0.92 GB process taking 17 ms. Cost scales with mapped/resident pages, so the auditor's "tens of ms for a multi-hundred-GB training process" is if anything conservative. At 2 s + 5 s cadence that is roughly 10% of a core burned continuously in page-table walks, and the walk holds the target's mmap read lock for its duration -- on the user's own multi-GB training processes, which is exactly what ContentionMonitor exists to protect.

Path frequency test passes: these are always-on daemon loops in the running console, not a cold path. The PSS metric itself is a documented design decision (memory note tomosar-ram-attribution) and the auditor correctly excludes it; the finding is the unthrottled rate and the duplication, which is not covered by any known non-issue. Tests (tests/webui/test_active_users.py) only assert metric semantics (`attributed <= rss`, share bounds) and monkeypatch the sample loops away, so nothing encodes the current cadence as intended behaviour.
correction:
Two details are off, and one source is missing.

1. "for EVERY pid on the box (not just the current user's)" overstates the kernel cost. The loop does call `attributed()` for every pid, but `/proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup` is ptrace-gated: for another user's process the open fails with EPERM and `attributed` falls back to the cheap `/proc/<pid>/statm` read (proc_stats.py:29-43). Measured here: 364 pids, only 142 successful rollup reads (all own). The expensive address-space walks are limited to the current user's processes -- which on a training box are precisely the multi-hundred-GB jobs, so the substance of the finding stands. The claimed "several hundred full address-space walks per second" is nearer ~100/s of real walks (~250/s of attempted opens).

2. A third, uncited source of the same cost: webui/system_monitor.py:130 `SystemMonitor._procs` calls `ProcStats.pss` on the top 30 processes on every `/api/system` request, and webui/static/js/home.js:156 polls that endpoint every 250 ms while the home tab is visible (with an in-flight guard). That adds up to ~120 rollup reads/s on a per-request handler path, on top of the two scanners. Any fix should cover all three call sites (a short-TTL cache in `ProcStats`, or one shared scanner feeding both monitors).

Cited lines are correct: system_monitor.py:464 and contention_monitor.py:270.

title: Four independent monitors each shell out to nvidia-smi; roughly 3-4 subprocess spawns per second, forever
description: There is no shared/cached GPU snapshot. `SystemHistory.sample_loop` runs `_gpu_devices()` every 0.5 s (1 nvidia-smi/0.5 s); `ActiveUsers.sample_loop` runs `gpu_occupancy()` every 2 s, which is 2 nvidia-smi calls (`_gpu_devices` + `_compute_apps`); `GpuWatchdog._watch` (gpu_watchdog.py:92) runs `gpu_occupancy()` every 4 s, another 2 calls; and `GpuSchedule` adds more per tick via `GpuAvailability.busy()`/`idle()`, each of which calls `gpu_occupancy()` again (gpu_schedule.py:111 and 119 — `_all_taken` plus one `grant` per live job). That is a sustained ~3.5 process spawns per second, each of which initialises the NVML driver context, plus a burst per schedule tick. `/api/system` adds one more `gpu_occupancy()` per poll.
suggested_fix: Put one short-TTL (e.g. 1 s) cached `gpu_occupancy()` on SystemMonitor behind its lock and have SystemHistory, ActiveUsers, GpuWatchdog and GpuAvailability all read it, instead of each spawning nvidia-smi on its own cadence.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. webui/system_monitor.py has no caching of the nvidia-smi result: _gpu_devices() (:135) and _compute_apps() (:165) each spawn nvidia-smi on every call, and gpu_occupancy() (:217) calls both. Three unconditionally-started loops hit them forever: SystemHistory.sample_loop at SAMPLE_PERIOD_S=0.5 (:366, thread started at :36) calls _gpu_devices() = 2 spawns/s; ActiveUsers.sample_loop at 2.0 s (:425, thread at :37) calls gpu_occupancy() via _gpu_by_user() (:490) = 1 spawn/s; GpuWatchdog._watch at INTERVAL=4.0 (gpu_watchdog.py:92, started from web_ui_server.py:151) calls gpu_occupancy() = 0.5 spawns/s. Sustained background total is exactly the claimed 3.5 process spawns per second. I measured the two queries on this machine at 34.9 ms and 22.0 ms (20-run average, single GPU), i.e. roughly 11% of a core burned continuously here, and nvidia-smi cost scales with device count on the 4-GPU server. This is a permanently-running background path plus a per-request handler, not a cold path, so the inefficiency criterion is met. No test encodes per-call freshness as intended behaviour (tests/webui/test_system_history.py:34 merely monkeypatches _gpu_devices), and this is not among the deliberate GPU-orchestration designs (intrusion ordering, charity mode, VRAM reservation).
correction: Two mechanism details in the claim are wrong, in opposite directions. (1) The GpuSchedule contribution is overstated: GpuAvailability.idle() (gpu_schedule.py:119) is reached only from _all_taken, which runs only when charity is enabled (DEFAULTS["charity"] is False) AND a bounce is pending; grant()->busy() (:111) runs from _cross only on a phase transition and from sweep() only every SWEEP_INTERVAL=600 s for jobs with withheld GPUs. There is no per-tick burst in the default configuration. (2) The /api/system contribution is understated: request_router.py:542 calls system.snapshot(), which calls gpu_occupancy() = 2 spawns per request, and webui/static/js/home.js:156 polls /api/system every 250 ms.
