An open home tab therefore adds 8 spawns/s, more than doubling the 3.5/s background rate, and since _Server is a ThreadingHTTPServer (web_ui_server.py:43) each additional open tab multiplies it again. The correct fix anchor is a short-TTL shared snapshot (e.g. 0.5 s) behind gpu_occupancy()/_gpu_devices(), which would collapse all consumers onto one nvidia-smi pair per period.

title: Own CPU/IO rate is a delta of a sum over a changing process set, so it drops to zero whenever one of the user's processes exits
description: `_scan` accumulates `jiffies` and `io_bytes` across all of the current user's pids and `prev_mine` holds the previous total. When any of those processes exits between samples the new total is smaller, `max(0.0, ...)` clamps the rate to 0.0, and `cpu.mine_share`/`io.mine_share` read 0 % for that cycle. That is exactly the moment a heavy job of the user finishes, so the "you are the cause" verdict and the dominance highlight in home.js flip off spuriously; the value also feeds `_check_nuke` through `_raise`'s latched `mine` flag. SystemMonitor._procs (system_monitor.py:104-108) gets this right by keeping per-pid previous jiffies. Related silent clip on line 135: `io_mbs` is derived from `/proc/<pid>/io`, which counts bytes across all block devices and network filesystems, while `disk["total_mbs"]` is one device from /proc/diskstats, so `io_share` can legitimately exceed 1 and is quietly `min(...)`-ed to 1.0 rather than flagged as unattributable.
evidence:
cpu_pct = max(0.0, 100.0 * (jiffies - prev[0]) / self.clk / dt)
            io_mbs  = max(0.0, (io_bytes - prev[1]) / dt / (1024.0 ** 2))
suggested_fix: Keep per-pid previous counters (as SystemMonitor._procs does) and sum the per-pid deltas over the pids present in both samples, so a process exiting removes only its own contribution instead of zeroing the whole rate.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. webui/contention_monitor.py:241-297: _scan accumulates `jiffies` and `io_bytes` over whichever of the user's pids exist at that instant and stores only the scalar pair in self.prev_mine (line 287); lines 292-293 subtract two sums taken over different process sets. Concrete failure: user has three ~100% CPU trainings; a job that ran one hour holds ~360000 lifetime jiffies (SC_CLK_TCK=100). It exits between samples; the two survivors contribute ~1000 jiffies over the 5 s interval, so jiffies - prev[0] = -359000, max(0.0, ...) forces cpu_pct = 0.0. Then cpu.mine_share = 0.0 (line 136), cpu_mine = False (line 388), and _raise latches known["mine"] = False (line 450) while two jobs still saturate the machine; the alarm text renders "you use 0% of all cores (0% busy)" and home.js drops the is-dominant class and flips the verdict from "you are the cause" to "busy, not you" for that cycle. The io path fails the same way because /proc/<pid>/io read_bytes/write_bytes are lifetime totals, so any exiting I/O-heavy process of the user zeroes io_mbs. The auditor's cross-reference holds and is in fact doubled: SystemMonitor._procs (system_monitor.py:104-108, per-pid prev_proc dict pruned by `seen`) and ActiveUsers._scan (system_monitor.py:460-468, sum of max(0, jiff - prev[pid]) per pid) both compute this exact quantity correctly in the same package, so the summed-total form is an inconsistency rather than house style. No test covers contention_monitor.py (grep "contention" hits only contention_monitor.py, request_router.py, web_ui_server.py, static/js/home.js, config_descriptions.json). Not one of the listed known non-issues. Severity is overstated though: the error is one-sided (new processes start at zero jiffies, so it can only undercount, never inflate), self-corrects after one 5 s cycle since the next sample rebaselines, and barely touches auto-nuke — _check_nuke requires level == "danger" while the CPU signal is hardcoded "warn" (line 389), and the memory signal that actually drives nukes uses instantaneous per-process memory and is immune; only the io flag is exposed, and only under psi.io.full >= 3, where the effect is to suppress a legitimate nuke rather than fire a spurious one. The secondary min(io_share, 1.0) point I do not confirm as a separate defect: the same clip is applied to mem_share and cpu_share (lines 134-136) and feeds a 0-100% gauge bar in home.js, so it is deliberate display normalization.
correction: Mechanism and location are correct (webui/contention_monitor.py:292-293, state kept at line 287, set in _scan lines 241-297). Corrections: (1) The auto-nuke consequence is much weaker than described — _check_nuke (line 405) only counts entries with level == "danger", and the CPU signal is hardcoded "warn" at line 389, so a spurious cpu zero can never gate a nuke; the memory signal, which is the main nuke driver, uses instantaneous per-process memory and is unaffected. Only the io `mine` flag reaches _check_nuke, and the failure direction is suppression of a warranted nuke, never a spurious one. (2) The error is strictly one-sided and lasts a single 5 s cycle, since the next sample rebaselines on the reduced total. (3) The secondary point about min(io_share, 1.0) on line 135 is not a separate defect: mem_share and cpu_share get the identical clip on lines 134 and 136 and all three feed a 0-100% gauge bar in home.js, so it is display normalization, not a silent swallow. Fix is the per-pid dict already used at system_monitor.py:104-108 and 460-468.

title: An alarm that starts as somebody else's and later becomes yours never logs or records the transition
description: `_raise` only appends to `self.events` and only calls `logger.warning` on the first raise, and only when `mine` is true at that instant. If contention is first detected while a neighbour is the dominant consumer (mine=False), `self.active[kind]` is created silently; on a later cycle when the user's own share crosses SHARE, the `else` branch just overwrites `known["mine"] = mine` — no event is appended to the history deque and nothing is logged. The transition from "the box is busy, not you" to "you are now the cause" is precisely the event the neighbour-impact monitor exists to record, and it is the only case the audit trail misses. The `_drop` side has the mirror problem: it logs "contention cleared" only if the alarm was mine at the moment it cleared.
evidence:
else:
                known["level"]   = level
                known["mine"]    = mine
                known["message"] = message
suggested_fix: Compare `known["mine"]` with the incoming `mine` in the else branch and, on a False->True transition, append the event and emit the warning exactly as the first-raise path does.
verdict_notes:
Traced from source in /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/webui/contention_monitor.py.

Mechanism, concretely: `_evaluate` computes e.g. `mem_mine = mem["mine_share"] >= self.SHARE` and calls `_track("mem", ...)` every INTERVAL (5 s). Once `self.streaks["mem"] >= SUSTAIN`, `_track` calls `_raise` on EVERY subsequent breached cycle. In `_raise` (lines 440-451) the alarm dict is keyed by `kind` alone. First raise with a neighbour dominant (mine=False) takes the `if known is None` branch, stores the entry, and skips both `self.events.append(...)` and `self.logger.warning("neighbour impact: ...")` because they are inside `if mine:`. Every later cycle takes the `else` branch, which only mutates `known["level"] / known["mine"] / known["message"]`. So the mem alarm entry silently flips `mine: False -> True` with no deque event and no log line. The alarm is not re-created in between because `_drop` only fires when the resource actually clears (with CLEAR_MARGIN hysteresis), so a long contention episode where the culprit changes from the neighbour to the user produces zero audit record of the moment the user became the cause.

The mirror asymmetry in `_drop` (lines 453-457) is also real and works in both directions: an alarm raised while mine=False and cleared while mine=True logs "contention cleared: mem" with no matching raise line; an alarm raised while mine=True and cleared after mine flipped to False logs the raise but never the clear.

Not a KNOWN NON-ISSUE — nothing in the project notes or code marks the events deque as "raise-time snapshot only", and there are no tests covering ContentionMonitor at all (grep for "contention" hits only contention_monitor.py, request_router.py, web_ui_server.py, config_descriptions.json, static/js/home.js).

Why I downgrade to minor rather than major: the live, user-facing verdict is driven by `state()["active"]` and `state()["impacting"] = any(a["mine"] ...)`, both of which read the mutated dict, so the home-page banner and the per-kind cards in `_renderImpact` (static/js/home.js) DO flip to "you are the cause" on the very next /api/system poll. `_check_nuke` likewise reads `self.active` and its `a["mine"]` flag, so armed auto-nuke still arms its streak correctly after the transition. What is lost is only the 20-entry `events` history (rendered as the last 3 lines in the panel) and the WebLogger warning line — an observability/audit gap, not a functional failure of the monitor or its kill path.
correction: Two details in the claim need adjusting. (1) The cited line 448 is the `else:` keyword; the substantive gap spans lines 445-451 (the `if mine:` guard on the first-raise branch plus the silent `else` update). (2) "it is the only case the audit trail misses" is inaccurate — the same `else` branch also swallows level escalations, so an alarm that starts `warn` and later becomes `danger` while already mine=True is likewise never appended to `events` nor logged. Severity is monitoring-only: the active-alarm state, the UI verdict banner, and the auto-nuke streak all observe the transition correctly; only the history deque and the log line miss it.

title: Incidents are never pruned: critical intrusions stay "active" forever and the dict grows without bound
description: `_register` inserts one entry per (gpu_uuid, intruder_pid) into `self.incidents` (line 180) and nothing ever deletes from that dict — `_escalate` only rewrites `status`. `state()` reports every incident whose status is "active" OR "critical", so once a critical is flagged it is returned in `active` on every `/api/system` poll for the lifetime of the server; home.js `_renderGpuGuard` renders it as a live critical card and there is no acknowledge/clear endpoint anywhere (`/api/gpu-guard/history` is read-only). The dict also grows monotonically with every distinct intruder pid ever seen, and `state()` scans all of it on every poll (~1 Hz).
evidence: active = [incident["record"] for incident in self.incidents.values() if incident["status"] in ("active", "critical")]
suggested_fix: Drop incidents in terminal states ("ended", "survived", and "critical" after it has been surfaced once) from `self.incidents` after a retention window, and/or add a POST endpoint to acknowledge a critical so the alarm panel can be cleared without restarting the console.
verdict_notes:
Reproduced from source. `/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/webui/gpu_watchdog.py`:

- `_register` (line 180) inserts `self.incidents[key] = {...}` keyed by `(gpu_uuid, intruder_pid)`; there is no `del self.incidents[...]` anywhere in the file (only `self.residents` is pruned, lines 149-151). `_escalate`/`_retire`/`_flag_critical` only rewrite `status`.
- `_escalate` (line 193) snapshots only incidents whose status is `"active"`, so once `_flag_critical` sets `status = "critical"` (line 231) the incident is never revisited: it can never transition to `"ended"` or `"survived"`.
- `state()` (line 50) returns every incident whose status is in `("active", "critical")`, so a critical incident is in the `active` payload forever.

Concrete failure: an intruder lands on a GPU I hold, one of my webui-tracked jobs exits nonzero within CRITICAL_WINDOW_S -> `_flag_critical` marks the incident critical. From that instant, every `/api/system` response (home.js polls at 250 ms, line 156) carries that record in `gpu_guard.active`. `home.js::_renderGpuGuard` (line ~899) renders it under the caption "live intrusions" as an `aint--critical` card, sets `is-firing`/`is-critical` on the alarm box and the header reads "gpu intrusion detected", while `_renderGuardPanel` reports `${crit} critical` instead of "all clear" (line ~961). This persists even after the intruder process and my jobs are long gone. There is no acknowledge/clear route: the only guard endpoints in `webui/request_router.py` are `/api/gpu-guard/history` (read-only, line 536) and the `/api/system` payload (line 545); nothing calls back into the watchdog to reset. Only a webui restart clears it, and the console is explicitly designed to be long-lived (detach/keep-alive).

Tests encode the stickiness only for the immediate post-crash scan (`tests/webui/test_gpu_watchdog.py:139-141`, `219-221`); no test asserts the critical incident ever clears, and there is no clearing path, so this is not a test-documented intent. It also cannot be argued as "the permanent record" design, since the permanent record already exists twice over: the journal (`intrusions.jsonl` via `_persist`, surfaced by `history()`) and the bounded `events` deque rendered as "recent events".

Where the auditor overstates: the unbounded-growth and per-poll-scan parts are near-meaningless. `incidents` only gains an entry per genuinely detected intrusion (a rare, human-scale event), each a small dict, and `state()` iterating a handful of entries at 4 Hz is not measurable. The real defect is the single stale-critical-alarm behaviour, which degrades the monitor's signal (the panel can never return to "all clear") rather than harming correctness of any job.

Also note a smaller related consequence worth mentioning: because a critical incident is skipped by `_escalate`, it never emits a `"survived"` record into `self.bounced`, so `GpuSchedule` charity mode never sees that intruder bounce. That is arguably desirable (no charity for someone whose arrival preceded your job's death) but it is a side effect of the same missing terminal-state handling, not an explicit decision.
correction: The mechanism is right (line 50 filter plus the missing terminal transition for `"critical"` in `_escalate` line 193), but the framing should be narrowed. The defect is: a critical incident has no exit path, so the home dashboard shows it as a live critical card indefinitely and the guard panel can never return to "all clear"; there is no acknowledge/clear endpoint. The "dict grows without bound" and "state() scans all of it on every poll" arguments do not carry weight — entries are only created on real intrusions (rare, tiny dicts) and the scan cost at 4 Hz is negligible. Severity is minor (stale monitoring UI on a single-user dev console), not major: no job, checkpoint, or scheduling decision is affected, aside from the critical incident never emitting a `"survived"` bounce record to `GpuSchedule` charity mode.

title: Autopsy profile plots run B's curve against run A's elevation axis without validating B's cube
description: `AbAutopsy.profile` reads `pred_a`, `pred_b` and `gt`, but only bounds-checks `az`/`rg` against `pred_a` and only derives `x_axis` from run A's `metrics.json` (`x_axis_min`/`x_axis_max`, sampled at `pred_a.shape[0]`). Nothing checks that `pred_b` has the same elevation length or the same x-axis extent. `webui/static/js/autopsy.js:113-116` draws `data.a`, `data.b` and `data.gt` against the single `data.x_axis`, so whenever the two runs were trained/inferred with a different elevation grid, run B's profile is silently rendered on the wrong axis — the exact comparison the tab exists to make. If B's cube is spatially smaller, `pred_b[:, az, rg]` raises IndexError, which is not in the caught tuple `(OSError, ValueError, FileNotFoundError, KeyError)` and escapes as a 500. `compare()` only validates the 2-D `pixel_mse` shapes, so it does not cover this.
evidence: if not (0 <= az < pred_a.shape[1] and 0 <= rg < pred_a.shape[2]):
suggested_fix: Validate `pred_b.shape == pred_a.shape` and that run B's `x_axis_min`/`x_axis_max` match run A's before returning; fail loudly with an explicit error message otherwise, and add IndexError to the caught tuple.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. webui/ab_autopsy.py:133-157: profile() bounds-checks az/rg against pred_a only (line 141) and builds x_axis from run A's metrics.json sampled at pred_a.shape[0] (line 145), then slices pred_b (line 153) with no shape or axis validation. webui/static/js/autopsy.js:113-117 passes the single data.x_axis into window.drawLineChart (webui/static/js/microscope.js:401-444), which maps every series through px(xAxis[i]) — so B is unavoidably drawn on A's axis. compare() only guards the 2-D pixel_mse shapes (line 112), which says nothing about the elevation dimension, so a pair with the same crop but a different elevation grid passes compare() and then silently mis-renders. The elevation axis is genuinely per-run: x_axis = GaussianAxis.build(gaussian_cfg.x_min, gaussian_cfg.x_max, layout.profile_length) (pipelines/backbone/training/pipeline.py:68), persisted in the checkpoint and reloaded at pipelines/backbone/inference/loader.py:114, with x_min/x_max from the dataset height_range (configuration/sar/gaussian_config.py:30). Decisive corroboration: the sibling cross-run comparison webui/cube_explorer.py:198-204 performs exactly the missing checks (full shape equality plus np.allclose on the elevation axis, erroring with "comparison cube covers a different elevation axis"), so this is an established project requirement that ab_autopsy skips — and skipping it produces a silently wrong result, which the repo's no-silent-fallback policy treats as a defect rather than tolerated behavior. tests/webui/test_ab_autopsy.py builds both stamps with identical N_ELEV and identical x_axis_min/max, so no test pins the mismatch case. Not one of the listed known non-issues.
correction: The core defect (B's curve rendered against A's elevation axis, unvalidated) is confirmed, but two details in the claim are off. (1) The IndexError path is practically unreachable through the UI: autopsy.js only calls /api/autopsy/profile after a successful compare(), and within a run pixel_mse is computed from the stitched curve cubes (pipelines/backbone/inference/predictor.py:316-330), so equal pixel_mse shapes imply equal pred_curves[1:] shapes. It is reachable only by hitting the endpoint directly. (2) It does not surface as a 500: neither RequestRouter.route nor _Handler.do_GET (webui/web_ui_server.py:53-57) wraps the call, so an escaping IndexError closes the connection with a traceback in the server log. The dominant, UI-reachable failure is the silent one: mismatched elevation length or extent raises no Python exception at all — a shorter pred_b is compressed onto A's grid, a longer one indexes xAxis past its end giving NaN coordinates and a silently truncated path. The fix belongs in profile(): validate pred_b.shape against pred_a.shape and compare B's own x_axis_min/x_axis_max against A's, mirroring webui/cube_explorer.py:198-204, and catch IndexError alongside the existing tuple at line 156.

title: Three model libraries insert configuration/architectures at sys.path[0] and import config modules under duplicate top-level names
description: `BackboneModelLibrary._import_backbone_models_config` (line 176-184), `ImageAutoencoderModelLibrary._import_image_autoencoder_models_config` (image_autoencoder_model_library.py:106-115) and `ProfileAutoencoderModelLibrary._import_profile_autoencoder_models_config` (profile_autoencoder_model_library.py:110-119) each do `sys.path.insert(0, <repo>/configuration/architectures)` and then `import backbone` / `import image_autoencoder` / `import profile_autoencoder`. These modules are already importable as `configuration.architectures.backbone` etc. (that is how `models/backbone/__init__.py` and `models/profile_autoencoder/__init__.py` reach them), so the effect is to load the same source file a second time under a second module name: `UNetConfig` from `backbone` and `UNetConfig` from `configuration.architectures.backbone` become distinct classes, and any future `isinstance`/identity check across the two would silently fail. It also permanently prepends a directory to `sys.path` ahead of `webui/` and the repo root for the whole server process, shadowing any future top-level module named `backbone`, `dual`, `unrolled`, `image_autoencoder` or `profile_autoencoder`. The project rule is that entry-point bootstrap code is the only place `sys.path` may be manipulated.
suggested_fix: Replace all three helpers with a plain `from configuration.architectures import backbone as backbone_config` (etc.) and delete the `sys` import from the three files.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source and empirically. webui/backbone_model_library.py:175-184, webui/image_autoencoder_model_library.py:106-116 and webui/profile_autoencoder_model_library.py:110-119 each insert <repo>/configuration/architectures at sys.path[0] and then import the config module under a bare top-level name. Running it confirms the double load: both 'backbone' and 'configuration.architectures.backbone' end up in sys.modules, UNetConfig from the two is not the same class (isinstance across them returns False), and sys.path[0] stays pointed at configuration/architectures for the rest of the process. The insert is redundant: configuration/architectures/__init__.py uses absolute imports, webui/serve.py:7 already puts the repo root on sys.path, and webui/fit_lab.py:14 imports configuration.param_extraction the normal way inside the same server; webui/jepa_model_library.py does no sys.path work at all, so the three libraries are also internally inconsistent. It violates the vault CLAUDE.md rule that entry-point bootstrap code is the only place sys.path manipulation is allowed - every other non-test insert lives in scripts/ bootstraps, webui/serve.py, or tools/sar/pyrat_env.py for the external PyRAT root. No test encodes the current behavior (tests/webui/test_backbone_model_library.py only checks registry/note coverage). This is not a known non-issue: it is not entry-point bootstrap, not a deferred main/ import, and not the intentional fit_lab JAX ordering.
correction: Severity should be minor, not major. The mechanism is real but the consequences are latent, not an active failure. _resolve_defaults in all three libraries only instantiates the config dataclass and reads activation/normalization (embedding_norm for the profile AE); nothing compares objects across the two module copies with isinstance or identity, and webui/config_registry.py reads config definitions by AST parsing rather than import, so no current code path misbehaves. No module named backbone, dual, unrolled, image_autoencoder or profile_autoencoder exists at top level elsewhere in the repo or in the Dune environment, so nothing is actually shadowed today. The confirmed harms are: (1) duplicate class identities that will silently break any future cross-module isinstance/identity check, (2) permanent global sys.path pollution ahead of webui/ and the repo root for the whole server process, mutated lazily from an HTTP worker thread on the first /api/models request, and (3) a direct violation of the project's sys.path rule. Fix is a one-line change in each of the three files to `from configuration.architectures import backbone` (respectively image_autoencoder, profile_autoencoder) with no path manipulation. Cited line numbers are accurate.

title: Training flow documents sorted_gt as the default param matching; the actual default is hungarian
description: The `paramterms` step of the backbone training flow tells the user that slot matching defaults to sorted-GT positional matching. `LossConfig.param_matching` defaults to `ParamMatching.HUNGARIAN`, `AblationCatalog.PARAM_MATCH_FULL = ParamMatching.HUNGARIAN`, and both the warmup and complete stages of `default_curriculum()` in configuration/training/backbone.py set `param_matching = AblationCatalog.PARAM_MATCH_FULL`. webui/equation_library.py:844 states the opposite (and correct) fact, so the two curated libraries rendered by the same web console contradict each other on the single most consequential loss switch. The Flows tab is the walkthrough new readers are pointed at, so it teaches the wrong permutation semantics (fixed height-rank slots vs permutation-invariant assignment).
evidence: "note": "The default sorted-GT matching orders GT slots by mu among active components (inactive amplitudes < 1e-3 pushed to the end); inactive slots mask their mu and sigma to zero so empty slots contribute amplitude only.
suggested_fix: Rewrite the note to describe hungarian (optimal-assignment) matching as the default, mentioning sorted_gt as the alternative, matching the wording already in equation_library.py:844.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. webui/flow_library.py:608, inside FlowLibrary._training() (the backbone training flow, lines 482-664), tells the reader "The default sorted-GT matching...". The actual default is HUNGARIAN at every level: LossConfig.param_matching = ParamMatching.HUNGARIAN (configuration/training/general/loss.py:50), AblationCatalog.PARAM_MATCH_FULL = ParamMatching.HUNGARIAN (configuration/training/general/ablation.py:12), and both the warmup and complete stages of default_curriculum() set param_matching = AblationCatalog.PARAM_MATCH_FULL (configuration/training/backbone.py:23 and :33). Dual pins HUNGARIAN too (configuration/training/dual.py:21-22); only JEPA defaults to SORTED_GT (configuration/training/jepa.py:24), and that belongs to a different flow (_jepa_train, lines 922-1045), so it cannot excuse the wording here. tools/loss/param_loss.py confirms the semantic difference: _match_hungarian calls _sort_gt then _assign_pred_to_gt (brute-force optimal assignment over all K! permutations), while _match_sorted_gt calls only _sort_gt. Hence the mu-sorting the note describes is common to both modes, and the note both mislabels the default and omits the prediction-permutation step that the real default performs; the words "hungarian"/"permutation" never appear in the training flow (grep over flow_library.py hits only line 1276, in the inference flow). webui/equation_library.py:844 states the correct fact explicitly, so the two curated libraries served by the same web console contradict each other. No test covers flow_library content (no tests/webui/test_flow_library.py; "paramterms" appears only in flow_library.py:607 and webui/static/js/flow_sketches.js:776, whose tip text is neutral and not wrong). This is not one of the listed known non-issues.
correction: Line and mechanism are right; severity is overstated. This is a curated documentation/UI-text defect with zero runtime effect — no code path reads the note to configure the loss, so no run behaves differently. Two details to add to the finding: (1) the mu-sorting with inactive slots pushed to the tail that the note describes is performed in BOTH matching modes (ParamMatcher._sort_gt is called by both _match_hungarian and _match_sorted_gt), so the note's error is not only the word "default" but also the omission of _assign_pred_to_gt, the K!-enumeration prediction permutation that is the whole point of the actual default; (2) the training flow never mentions Hungarian matching anywhere, so the fix is to rewrite the note rather than swap one adjective. Suggested minimal wording: "The default hungarian matching sorts GT slots by mu among active components (inactive amplitudes < 1e-3 pushed to the end) and then permutes each pixel's predicted slots onto the GT slots by the optimal assignment; under the opt-in sorted_gt mode predictions keep their slot order. Inactive slots mask their mu and sigma to zero..." Also worth noting for the same note: it quotes the inactive-amplitude threshold as 1e-3, which matches ParamMatcher.ACTIVE_AMP_THR (tools/loss/param_loss.py:10) but not LossConfig.amp_zero_thr = 1e-4 (configuration/training/general/loss.py); that is a separate, smaller ambiguity, not part of this finding.

title: amp_zero_thr documented as 1e-3 in four places; every config default is 1e-4
description: Both curated libraries state that the active-slot amplitude threshold `amp_zero_thr` is 1e-3. The real defaults are `LossConfig.amp_zero_thr = 1e-4` (configuration/training/general/loss.py:59) and `ProfileDatasetConfig.amp_zero_thr = 1e-4` (configuration/dataset/profile_autoencoder.py:33), and those are the values threaded into `ParamMatcher.match(..., active_thr=...)`, the mu/sigma activity mask, presence balancing, `ParamSampler`/`SlotVitals`, and the profile-AE active-pixel gate. The docs are off by a factor of 10 on the threshold that decides which Gaussian slots are supervised. Locations: equation_library.py:98 (per-pixel parameter vector), equation_library.py:861 (tau_a in the activity-mask card), flow_library.py:699 (profile-AE active-pixel gate note) and flow_library.py:702 (the accompanying tex literal `\tau_a = 10^{-3}`). Note the separate constants that genuinely ARE 1e-3 (`ParamMatcher.ACTIVE_AMP_THR` used by the inference metrics, and `stats_computer` amp_threshold) are what the text appears to have been conflated with.
evidence: and a slot counts as active when its amplitude exceeds amp_zero_thr = 1e-3.
suggested_fix: Change all four to 1e-4, and where the 1e-3 inference-side ACTIVE_AMP_THR is meant, say so explicitly so the two thresholds are not merged.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. configuration/training/general/loss.py:59 sets LossConfig.amp_zero_thr = 1e-4 and configuration/dataset/profile_autoencoder.py:33 sets ProfileDatasetConfig.amp_zero_thr = 1e-4. Those values are what actually flow through the code: pipelines/backbone/training/loss.py lines 103, 135, 233 build the activity mask and presence weights from cfg.amp_zero_thr, and line 158 explicitly passes active_thr=self.loss_cfg.amp_zero_thr into ParamMatcher.match, so the class-level ParamMatcher.ACTIVE_AMP_THR = 1e-3 (tools/loss/param_loss.py:10) never applies during training; trainer.py:73-74 threads the same value into ParamSampler and SlotVitals; and pipelines/profile_autoencoder/dataset/datasets.py:58 gates active pixels with the dataset config value. Meanwhile the curated webui docs assert 1e-3 in exactly the four cited places: webui/equation_library.py:98 ("a slot counts as active when its amplitude exceeds amp_zero_thr = 1e-3"), webui/equation_library.py:861 (tau_a desc "amp_zero_thr = 1e-3"), webui/flow_library.py:699 ("A pixel is active when any component amplitude exceeds amp_zero_thr = 1e-3") and the tex literal at flow_library.py:702 (\tau_a = 10^{-3}). The auditor's diagnosis of conflation is also correct: ParamMatcher.ACTIVE_AMP_THR (used by inference metrics, slot_organization, failure_modes, normalization_audit, layer_probes) and stats_computer.py:284 amp_threshold genuinely are 1e-3. The neighbouring doc text quotes real defaults correctly (keep_empty_frac = 0.05, pixel_subsample default 1.0, param_weights (1,1,1)), so the convention is clearly to mirror config defaults and these four are a 10x error. No test cross-checks the curated libraries against the config dataclasses (tests/webui/ has no equation/flow library test), which explains the drift. This is not one of the known non-issues. One detail the auditor left out: webui/launch_layout.py:130 does set "curriculum.complete.amp_zero_thr": "0.001" in the Legacy preset (asserted by tests/webui/test_launch_layout.py:110), so 1e-3 is a legitimate value for that one preset -- but the docs claim it as the general/default threshold, which is wrong. Severity should be minor rather than major: the defect is confined to display strings in two curated documentation libraries; no runtime path reads them, no training or inference behaviour changes, and no artifact is mis-written. Category is better described as documentation drift than unintended behaviour.
correction: Claim is factually accurate at all four cited locations, but severity should be minor, not major: the impact is documentation-only (curated webui equation/flow library strings shown on the Model page), with no runtime, training, or artifact consequence. Category is documentation drift rather than unintended behaviour. Two additions: (1) webui/launch_layout.py:130 legitimately sets "curriculum.complete.amp_zero_thr": "0.001" for the Legacy preset (locked in by tests/webui/test_launch_layout.py:110), so 1e-3 is a valid value for that one preset -- the docs err by presenting it as the general default; (2) the drift persists because nothing tests the curated libraries against the config dataclasses -- tests/webui/ contains no equation_library or flow_library test. Fix: change 1e-3 -> 1e-4 at equation_library.py:98, equation_library.py:861, flow_library.py:699, and the tex literal \tau_a = 10^{-3} -> 10^{-4} at flow_library.py:702, and consider a test that asserts the documented threshold equals LossConfig.amp_zero_thr / ProfileDatasetConfig.amp_zero_thr.

title: Flow library quotes bare sub-config defaults that ConfigFactory always overrides (T, patience, eval frequency, weight decay)
description: Several training flows document the standalone dataclass defaults rather than the values every run actually gets. `TrainingQueueConfig` (configuration/training/general/run.py) sets epochs=60, validation_frequency=1 and early_stop_patience=30, and `ConfigFactory` (pipelines/shared/config/config_factory.py:80-88) installs `scheduler.epochs = scheduler_epochs or epochs`, i.e. 60 — not the SchedulerConfig standalone 100. Effective weight decay is the per-group 1e-4 from `get_param_groups`, not `OptimizerConfig.weight_decay = 0.1` (which is only a setdefault fallback no architecture config hits — a nuance equation_library.py:1164 and config_descriptions.json both get right). Affected locations: flow_library.py:645 (`T=100`), :654 ("every 5 epochs", "after 15 evaluations"), :634 ("decoupled weight decay 0.1"), :786 and :789 (`T = 100` in profile-AE note and tex), :806 (`patience = 15`), :903 (`T = 100` in image-AE tex), :909 and :912 ("every 5 epochs", "patience = 15"). The profile-AE and image-AE entries route through the same TrainingQueueConfig, so they inherit the same 60/1/30 values.
evidence: "note": "Each group's effective LR is its base rate times the per-epoch cosine factor (T=100, eta_min=1e-6) times the per-step warmup factor (200 steps from start factor 0.1);
suggested_fix: Quote the effective entry-point values (T=60, validation every epoch, patience 30, per-group weight decay 1e-4) and, where useful, note the bare dataclass default in parentheses as equation_library already does.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. TrainingQueueConfig (configuration/training/general/run.py:30-40) defaults epochs=60, scheduler_epochs=None, validation_frequency=1, early_stop_patience=30. ConfigFactory.training_trainer_config (pipelines/shared/config/config_factory.py:75-99) installs SchedulerConfig(epochs=scheduler_epochs or epochs)=60, EarlyStoppingConfig(patience=30) and TrainingLoopConfig(validation_frequency=1), so the standalone dataclass values (SchedulerConfig.epochs=100, TrainingLoopConfig.validation_frequency=5, EarlyStoppingConfig.patience=15 in optimization.py:42,60 and runtime.py:25) are never what a default run gets. Profile-AE and image-AE pipelines build on that same base and then inherit_shared_from(base) copies scheduler/early_stopping/training wholesale (configuration/training/general/trainer.py:3-12), so they inherit 60/1/30 as well; their entry configs only change batch_size/num_workers. Weight decay: tools/training/trainer.py:186-191 only setdefaults OptimizerConfig.weight_decay=0.1, and every get_param_groups in configuration/architectures/*.py sets weight_decay explicitly per group, so 0.1 is unreachable. The flow notes at lines 634 ("weight decay 0.1"), 645 ("T=100"), 654 ("every 5 epochs", "after 15 evaluations"), 786/789 (T = 100), 806 ("patience = 15"), 900/903 ("T = scheduler.epochs = 100"), 909/912 ("every 5", "patience = 15") therefore document values no default run uses. webui/equation_library.py:1035,1057,1068,1080 already documents the correct 60-vs-100 distinction, confirming the flow library is the stale surface rather than the intended one; no test in tests/webui asserts flow_library content, so the wrong numbers are not encoded as intended behavior. Trainer usage confirms the fields matter as documented (tools/training/trainer.py:439 do_eval on validation_frequency; tools/training/stopping.py:10,34 counts validation rounds against patience).
correction: Category is documentation accuracy, not runtime "unintended-behavior": nothing in the training path misbehaves, only the webui Model-page flow narration is stale, so major overstates it. Two detail fixes: (1) effective weight decay is the per-group *_wd value, which is 1e-4 for the standard UNet/ResUNet families but 5e-3 or 1e-2 for some others (grep over configuration/architectures/*.py: 58 groups at 1e-4, 10 at 5e-3, 8 at 1e-2, 1 at 0.0) — the right correction is "per-group weight decay (1e-4 for the standard families)", not a flat 1e-4. (2) At line 806 the note's phrase "Every validation_frequency epochs" is already correct; only the trailing "patience = 15" is wrong there. Also add line 900 to the affected list ("T = scheduler.epochs = 100" in the image-AE note, not just the tex on 903). title: Patch geometry documented as square 64x64 with a single stride 32, contradicting the settled rectangular (az, rg) convention
description: `PatchConfig` is `size = (64, 32)`, `stride = (32, 16)` (configuration/dataset/general/dataset.py:170-173) and `Patcher.build` (pipelines/backbone/dataset/spatial.py:171-181) unpacks two independent strides `sv, sh`. Both curated libraries still describe one scalar stride and square patches: equation_library.py:491-492 gives "patch size, default (64, 64)" and "stride, default 32"; equation_library.py:486 and :498 write the grid and padding formulas with a single `s` for both axes; flow_library.py:378 does the same (`n_v = ceil((A_z - P_H)/s) + 1, n_h = ceil((R_g - P_W)/s) + 1`); flow_library node shapes are written `C x P x P` / `B x C_in x P x P` throughout (lines 326, 484, 821, 924, 1142, 1463); and the worked sample at flow_library.py:325 (`n_v=89, n_h=93`) only reproduces with a square stride 32 — with the real rg stride 16 the range count is 186.
evidence:
{"sym": r"P_H, P_W", "desc": "patch size, default (64, 64)"},
{"sym": r"s",        "desc": "stride, default 32"},
suggested_fix: Split the stride into `s_v, s_h` in both tex formulas, set the documented defaults to (64, 32) and (32, 16), replace `P x P` shapes with `P_H x P_W`, and recompute the n_h sample.
verdict_notes:
I reproduced every element of the claim from source.

Code side (ground truth is per-axis):
- /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/configuration/dataset/general/dataset.py:170-173 — `PatchConfig.size = (64, 32)`, `stride = (32, 16)`.
- /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/configuration/training/general/run.py:73-74 and configuration/training/unrolled.py:39-40 — `patch_size = (64, 32)`, `patch_stride = (32, 16)`; configuration/training/backbone.py:159-160 is `(32, 32)`/`(16, 16)`. No config anywhere defaults to `(64, 64)` with a scalar stride 32.
- /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/pipelines/backbone/dataset/spatial.py:174-181 — `Patcher.build` unpacks `ph, pw = patch_size` and `sv, sh = stride`, then computes `n_v = ceil((H-ph)/sv)+1`, `n_h = ceil((W-pw)/sh)+1`, `pad_v = ph + (n_v-1)*sv - H`, `pad_h = pw + (n_h-1)*sh - W`. Two genuinely independent strides.
- webui/config_descriptions.json:290-291 already describes both fields correctly as per-axis tuples, so the rest of the webui documentation surface agrees with the code — the drift is isolated to the two curated math/flow libraries.

Documentation side (wrong):
- webui/equation_library.py:486 writes the grid with a single `s` on both axes; :491-492 declare "patch size, default (64, 64)" and "stride, default 32"; :498 and :504 repeat the single `s` in the padding formula; :517 again for patch corners. Line 1270 likewise writes the stitching blend window with one `P`.
- webui/flow_library.py:378 and :387 repeat the single-`s` grid and padding formulas; :375 says "a regular strided grid of PxP patches"; node shapes are `C x P x P` / `C_in x P x P` at lines 326-336, 484-491, 821-825 (and further down).
- The worked sample at flow_library.py:325 (`n_v=89, n_h=93`) on the sample split `(0, 2867, 0, 3000)` only reproduces with square (64,64)/(32,32); I ran the arithmetic: square gives exactly (89, 93), while the real rectangular default (64,32)/(32,16) gives (89, 187). So the sample was authored against the pre-rectangular convention.

I looked for a refutation and found none: no test asserts these strings (tests/webui has no equation_library/flow_library test; only webui/request_router.py, web_ui_server.py and README reference them), so nothing pins the square wording as intended. launch_layout.py:141 / tests/webui/test_launch_layout.py:122 do carry `training.patch_size = "(64, 64)"`, but that is one named preset's explicit override, not a claim about the default, so it does not rescue the "default (64, 64)" wording. This is also not one of the listed known non-issues — the per-axis rectangular exemption in the non-issue list is the Capon boxcar window (w_a x w_r), a different concept; the rectangular (az, rg) patch convention is a settled project decision the docs simply failed to follow.

Two corrections to the auditor's write-up: the range count under the real defaults is 187, not 186 (ceil(2968/16)+1 = 187), and the category is documentation drift rather than unintended behavior — no runtime path is wrong, only the curated explanatory pages the webui renders. Real, reproducible, but doc-only.
correction:
Mechanism confirmed, two details corrected.

1) Arithmetic: with the real defaults (size (64,32), stride (32,16)) the sample split (0, 2867, 0, 3000) yields n_h = ceil((3000-32)/16)+1 = 187, not 186. n_v = 89 is unchanged, which is why the square-config value 93 is the only way to get the documented sample.

2) Category/severity: this is documentation drift in curated webui content, not unintended runtime behavior. `Patcher.build` (pipelines/backbone/dataset/spatial.py:174-181) is correct and honours per-axis strides; nothing computes a wrong patch grid. The defect is confined to the two hand-written libraries that the Model/Equations pages render, so severity is minor rather than major.

Scope is also slightly wider than stated: besides the cited lines, equation_library.py:517 uses a single `s` for the patch-corner formula and equation_library.py:1270 writes the stitching blend window with a single `P` (`w_v[i] = 1 - |2(i+0.5)/P - 1|`) despite the window being built per-axis. Fix list: equation_library.py:486, 491-492, 498, 504, 517, 1270; flow_library.py:325 (sample n_h), 375, 378, 387, and the `C x P x P` / `B x C_in x P x P` node shapes at 326-336, 484-491, 821-825 and later occurrences. Correct defaults to size (64, 32) and stride (32, 16), and split `s` into `s_v, s_h`.

Note that webui/config_descriptions.json:290-291 already documents both fields as per-axis tuples, so the rest of the webui surface is consistent with the code — only these two curated libraries were missed by the 2026-07-14 rectangular-patch migration.

title: The param_legacy loss term is missing from both curated libraries and the term count is stale
