The `max_workers is not None` branch is protected by `max(1, ...)`; the None branch is not, and `tests/orchestration/test_pool.py::test_empty_jobs_returns_empty` only covers the guarded branch (max_workers=2). The same expression also makes the None case unbounded: one OS process per job, however many jobs there are.
evidence: workers  = max(1, min(self.max_workers, len(job_list))) if self.max_workers is not None else len(job_list)
suggested_fix: Use `max(1, len(job_list))` (or `min(len(job_list), os.cpu_count())`) in the None branch, and return early when `job_list` is empty.
verdict_notes:
The mechanism is real and I reproduced it. /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/tools/orchestration/pool.py:17 reads `workers = max(1, min(self.max_workers, len(job_list))) if self.max_workers is not None else len(job_list)`. With `max_workers=None` (which is the constructor default, line 11) and an empty `jobs` iterable, `workers` is 0, and line 20 builds `ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=0, ...)`. Loading pool.py in isolation (stubbing only the Logger import) and calling `ProcessPoolRunner(logger, max_workers=None).run([], abs)` raises `ValueError: max_workers must be greater than 0` on this interpreter (CPython 3.12.3). The guarded branch is fine: `max(1, ...)` keeps it at 1 for an empty list, which is why tests/orchestration/test_pool.py:40 `test_empty_jobs_returns_empty` (max_workers=2) passes and does not cover the None path; the only None test, `test_unbounded_workers_when_none` (line 94), uses 2 jobs.

Two corrections to the claim's framing, though. First, reachability: no production call site can hit this. The only two constructions in the repo are pipelines/processing/generation/tomogram.py:101 (`max_workers=resolved_workers`, coming from `ParallelConfig.resolve_plan` in configuration/sar/processing_config.py:56, whose every return path is wrapped in `max(1, ...)` or a `range(1, ...)` search, so it is always >= 1) and pipelines/shared/orchestration/session_scheduler.py:36 (`max_workers=1`). So this is a latent API-surface defect on the public default, not a live crash on any executed path.

Second, the "unbounded" half of the claim is not a defect: tests/orchestration/test_pool.py:94 is literally named `test_unbounded_workers_when_none`, so one process per job when `max_workers is None` is the intended, test-encoded contract, not an oversight. Only the 0-worker edge is a genuine bug.
correction: Confirmed at the cited file and line (tools/orchestration/pool.py:17). Scope narrower than described: (a) unreachable from production — both call sites (tomogram.py:101 via ParallelConfig.resolve_plan, session_scheduler.py:36) always pass an int >= 1, so this only bites a caller that relies on the `max_workers: int | None = None` default with an empty job list; (b) the "unbounded workers" complaint should be dropped — tests/orchestration/test_pool.py:94 `test_unbounded_workers_when_none` encodes one-process-per-job as the intended contract for None. Fix is the one-token change of applying the same `max(1, ...)` to the None branch, e.g. `workers = max(1, min(self.max_workers, len(job_list)) if self.max_workers is not None else len(job_list))`, plus an empty-job test with max_workers=None. Severity stays minor (latent robustness, not a live failure).

title: Logger.save_profiler_results is never called
description: No caller anywhere in the repository (pipelines, main/, webui Python or JS, scripts, tests) references `save_profiler_results`, and no cProfile/pstats object is ever handed to a Logger. It is the sole reason logger.py depends on tools.reporting (see the related organization finding).
suggested_fix: Remove the method, or move it next to the profiling code that was supposed to call it and wire it up.
verdict_notes: Reproduced independently from source. tools/monitoring/logger.py:369 defines `save_profiler_results(self, stats, output)` exactly as quoted. A repo-wide grep for the symbol (all files, including tests/, main/, webui/static/js, and *.json registries such as script_catalog/launch_layout/config_descriptions/repomap_data) returns a single hit: the definition line itself. There is no string-form reference either. A grep for `cProfile`, `pstats`, and `profiler` over the whole repo hits only lines 369 and 389 of this same file, so no pstats.Stats object is ever built anywhere that could be passed as the `stats` argument (the method body requires `stats.stats.items()` with pstats-shaped tuples). No reflective dispatch exists: the only getattr on logging is `LOG_LEVELS = {name: getattr(logging, name) ...}` at line 122, and there is no `inspect.getmembers` or `dir(Logger)` anywhere; NullLogger.__getattr__ returns no-op lambdas but is not a caller. tests/monitoring/test_logger.py exercises 32 Logger behaviors and none reference this method, so no test encodes it as intended behavior. The dependency claim also holds: MarkdownDoc/MarkdownTable (imported line 28 from tools.reporting.markdown) are used only at lines 374 and 384, both inside this method. This is not covered by any of the listed known non-issues.
correction: Minor completion of the mechanism: the method is also the sole user of the `RunTag` import (line 29, `from tools.runtime.run_tag import RunTag`), used only at line 385. Removing the method would strip two imports — `tools.reporting.markdown` and `tools.runtime.run_tag` — not just the tools.reporting one the auditor cited. Cited line, file, and severity are otherwise accurate.

title: Resume reuses an inference produced for a different split
description: `_has_inference` returns True as soon as *any* subdirectory under `<item>/inference/` carries a completion marker. Inference output directories are named by `output_subdir` or by a timestamp (`pipelines/backbone/inference/run_metadata_paths.py:16`), never by the split. `QueuedInferenceStage._config_kv` advertises `self.config.inference.split`, so re-running a run tag with `--inference.split test` after a `val` inference exists logs "Split: test" and then "existing inference reused", and the downstream comparison/report consumes the old split's metrics. `FoldInferenceStage` had to work around exactly this by overriding with a split-aware `_has_split_inference`.
evidence: return any(CompletionMarker.is_complete(candidate) for candidate in inference_dir.iterdir() if candidate.is_dir())
suggested_fix: Key the reuse check on the configured split (as FoldInferenceStage does), or record the split inside the completion marker payload and compare it.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. `QueuedInferenceStage._has_inference` (tools/orchestration/stages.py:163-171) treats "any subdirectory under <item>/inference/ carrying complete.json" as a cache hit, with no split in the key. The benchmark inference worker builds its config through ConfigFactory.inference_config with `output_subdir=None` (pipelines/shared/config/config_factory.py:113), so InferenceMetadata names the output dir `RunTag.now()` (pipelines/backbone/inference/run_metadata_paths.py:16) — a timestamp, never the split. `inference.split` is a real user-settable field (configuration/benchmark/general.py:38, default "test") exposed in the benchmark launch form next to `run_tag` and `resume` (webui/launch_layout.py:379-386; `resume` defaults True at configuration/benchmark/general.py:105), and StagedPipeline reuses `log_base_dir/<run_tag>` when a tag is supplied, so rerunning the same tag with a different split takes the resume path: `_config_kv` prints "Split: <new>", every unit logs "existing inference reused", no worker runs, and no new inference is produced. Downstream, TrialCollector._attach_inference (pipelines/shared/comparison/trial_collection.py:136-152) picks the newest inference dir containing metrics.json regardless of split, and ComparisonReport never reads the `split` key that pipelines/backbone/inference/pipeline.py:121 writes, so the stale split's metrics are published under the new split's label. FoldInferenceStage._has_split_inference (pipelines/cross_validation/stages.py:73-77), paired with folds.py:156 setting `output_subdir = split`, shows the project does consider split part of the resume identity elsewhere — this is an inconsistency, not a deliberate design. Tests (tests/orchestration/test_stages.py:205-218) only encode the split-agnostic "any complete subdir reuses" rule and never exercise a changed split, so they do not sanction the mismatch. Not covered by any listed known non-issue: this is a silent reuse of mismatched artifacts, the opposite of the project's "break loudly" policy.
correction: Line and mechanism are correct; two additions. (1) The affected concrete consumer is pipelines/benchmark/stages.py:296 `InferenceStage` (the only subclass that does not override the check), reached via BenchmarkPipeline._run_inference; the downstream consumption point is pipelines/shared/comparison/trial_collection.py:136-152, which also selects the inference dir split-agnostically. (2) The split is in fact already persisted in the marker: pipelines/backbone/inference/pipeline.py:418-421 stamps `{"stage": "inference", "split": run.split_name}`, and metrics.json records `split` at line 121. So `_has_inference` discards information it already has on disk — the fix is to read the marker payload and require a split match, no new bookkeeping needed. The same blind reuse also ignores a changed `inference.checkpoint_name`, though split is the load-bearing case.

title: Weight x-ray series plots mix two different tensor index bases under the same axis label
description: `layer_l2_norm.png` and `layer_rank_ratio.png` are built from `weight_reports` (role == "weight" only) while `layer_std.png` and `layer_sparsity.png` are built from `reports` (all tensors: biases, norm scales, running_mean/var). All four use the same x-axis label "Tensor index (forward order)", so index i does not refer to the same tensor across the set, and `layer_std.png` is titled "Per-tensor weight dispersion" while plotting non-weight tensors.
evidence: self._series_plot([report.std       for report in reports],        "Standard deviation",   "Per-tensor weight dispersion",     "layer_std.png",       log_y=True),
suggested_fix: Use `weight_reports` consistently for the weight-titled plots (or retitle the all-tensor plots and give them their own axis label).
verdict_notes:
Reproduced from source, not from the auditor's summary.

/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/tools/diagnostics/weight_xray_plots.py `WeightXrayPlots.render` (lines 133-143) builds `weight_reports = [r for r in reports if r.role == "weight"]` and then feeds two series from `weight_reports` (l2_norm -> layer_l2_norm.png, rank_ratio -> layer_rank_ratio.png) and two from the unfiltered `reports` (std -> layer_std.png, frac_dead -> layer_sparsity.png).

`reports` is a strict superset. /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/tools/diagnostics/weight_xray_analysis.py `WeightAnalyzer.analyze_tensor` (lines 190-225) drops only `num_batches_tracked` counters, 0-dim tensors and non-floating tensors; everything else is kept with role in {"weight" (ndim>=2 and name ends in .weight), "norm_scale" (1-D .weight), "bias", "running_mean", "running_var", "other"}. So biases, BatchNorm/LayerNorm scales and running statistics are all in `reports` but not in `weight_reports`.

`_series_plot` (lines 48-77) plots against `enumerate(values)` — the position in the list it was handed — with a fixed x-label "Tensor index (forward order)" and integer ticks only, no tensor names. It preserves the index when a value is None (it filters points, not indices), which is exactly what makes indices comparable across plots; that design intent only holds if all series come from the same base list.

Concrete instance using the repo's own test fixture (/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/tests/diagnostics/test_weight_xray_plots.py, state_dict = encoder.blocks.0.conv.weight [16,8], encoder.blocks.0.conv.bias [16], decoder.head.weight [16,8]):
- weight_reports = [encoder.blocks.0.conv.weight, decoder.head.weight] -> in layer_l2_norm.png and layer_rank_ratio.png, x=1 is decoder.head.weight.
- reports = [encoder.blocks.0.conv.weight, encoder.blocks.0.conv.bias, decoder.head.weight] -> in layer_std.png and layer_sparsity.png, x=1 is encoder.blocks.0.conv.bias and decoder.head.weight moves to x=2.
So the reader who spots the rank collapse of the dead `decoder.head.weight` at x=1 in layer_rank_ratio.png reads x=1 in layer_std.png/layer_sparsity.png and gets the bias instead. With a real checkpoint (every conv/norm contributing bias + scale + running_mean + running_var), the offset grows monotonically along the network, so essentially no index above the first few refers to the same tensor across the two plot families.

Secondary confirmations of the claim's sub-points: layer_std.png is titled "Per-tensor weight dispersion" and layer_sparsity.png "Per-tensor dead-weight fraction" while both include running_mean/running_var/bias entries; `frac_dead` for a running_var tensor (values below `dead_abs_threshold`, see `_basic_stats` line 117) plotted against the `dead_fraction_warn` threshold line is not a weight-sparsity statement at all.

This is not one of the listed known non-issues (no legacy shim, no dynamic dispatch, not a settled SAR/plotting convention). The only test touching this code asserts filenames exist and titles wrap; nothing encodes an intent that the four plots use different bases. Note also that the `weight_reports` filter on the rank_ratio series is redundant — `rank_ratio` is None for every non-weight role and `_series_plot` already drops Nones — which is further evidence that the uniform base was meant to be `weight_reports` (or `reports`) for all four, and that lines 139-140 are the inconsistent ones.

Impact is confined to a cold offline diagnostics path (main/analysis/xray_weights.py -> WeightXray.run), and nothing downstream consumes the plots numerically (the report only embeds the PNGs and prints an exact per-tensor table). Misreading risk only, so "minor" is the right severity.
correction: The claim is accurate but should cite lines 139-140 (both `reports`-based series), not line 139 alone, and the mislabelled-title problem applies to layer_sparsity.png ("Per-tensor dead-weight fraction" over running_mean/running_var/bias) as well as layer_std.png. Worth adding that `_series_plot` deliberately preserves the enumerate index across dropped None values, which is what makes the shared "Tensor index (forward order)" label a cross-plot promise; and that the `weight_reports` filter on the rank_ratio series (line 141) is redundant since rank_ratio is None for all non-weight roles and Nones are already filtered — so the consistent fix is to source all four series from the same list (and either drop the "weight" wording from the std/sparsity titles or restrict them to weights).

title: Flagged-layer histograms are truncated in state-dict order, not by severity
description: `flagged` preserves state-dict iteration order, and the cap is applied by plain slicing. With the default `max_layer_histograms = 24`, a network with more than 24 flagged weight tensors silently drops the histograms of every later tensor — including `critical` ones — while plotting early `warning`-only tensors. The report's "Diagnostic plots" section then omits precisely the layers the verdict is about.
suggested_fix: Sort `flagged` by severity rank (critical first, then e.g. by frac_dead / |w|max) before slicing.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. WeightAnalyzer.analyze (tools/diagnostics/weight_xray_analysis.py:227) iterates state_dict.items() and appends, and IssueDetector.run mutates and returns the same list, so `reports` is in state-dict/forward order. WeightXrayPlots._flagged_histograms (weight_xray_plots.py:118) filters role=="weight" and severity in ("warning","critical") and line 119 truncates with a plain slice `flagged[: self.config.max_layer_histograms]` (default 24, configuration/diagnostics.py:52 and :102) with no severity key. The rest of the module proves the intended convention is severity-first: weight_xray_report.py:47-48 and :61-62 both sort flagged reports by ordering {"critical":0,"warning":1,"info":2} before rendering. Concrete failure: a checkpoint with >24 flagged weight tensors, e.g. many encoder convs warning on rank_deficient (rank_ratio<=0.50) or dead_neurons (dead_output_frac>=0.10), plus a late tensor such as decoder.head.weight flagged critical for rank_collapse or dead_tensor -> the critical tensor's histogram is never rendered while 24 warning-only encoder tensors are, and the report's "Diagnostic plots" section (weight_xray_report.py:115-118) shows only the early warnings. No test pins the ordering (tests/diagnostics/test_weight_xray_plots.py only asserts some layer_histograms file exists). Not one of the known non-issues.
correction: Two refinements. (1) Impact is narrower than stated: only the histogram PLOTS are dropped. The Findings table (_issue_table), the console flagged table, the per-tensor metrics table and weight_xray.json still list every flagged tensor, and the first two are severity-sorted, so the verdict evidence itself is not omitted from the report — only its visual companion. That keeps the severity at minor. (2) The identical severity-agnostic truncation exists a second place: pipelines/backbone/inference/activation_xray.py:62 (`for report in flagged[: self.config.max_layer_histograms]`, with `flagged` built in depth order at line 115) using default max_layer_histograms = 12 (configuration/diagnostics.py:235). A fix (sort by severity rank before slicing) should cover both call sites.

title: GpuQueue leaks log file handles and orphans running workers if run() raises
description: `_launch` opens the log file before `subprocess.Popen`; if Popen raises (bad interpreter/entry path, EMFILE) the handle is never closed and the exception escapes `run()`. `run()`'s `finally` only restores the signal handlers — it neither terminates the subprocesses still in `self.running` nor closes their `log_fh`. Any exception escaping the scheduling loop (`_reap`, `_reconcile`, `_publish_progress`, a logger failure) therefore leaves training workers running unsupervised on the GPUs, with open write handles, while the scheduler dies. Cleanup exists only on the signal path (`_terminate_running`) and on normal completion (`_reap`).
evidence:
log_fh  = open(job.log_path, "w", encoding="utf-8")
        process = subprocess.Popen(command, stdout=log_fh, stderr=log_fh)
suggested_fix: Wrap the Popen in try/except to close `log_fh` on failure, and extend `run()`'s `finally` to terminate/reap `self.running` and close every `log_fh` before re-raising.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. `_launch` (gpu_queue.py:315-324) opens the log handle at line 319 and calls `subprocess.Popen` at line 320 with no try/except, and `run()`'s `finally` (lines 375-376) executes only `self._restore_signal_handlers(previous_handlers)` — it never iterates `self.running`, never terminates the children, never closes `log_fh`. Child cleanup exists only in `_terminate_running` (220-236, bound to SIGTERM/SIGINT) and `_reap` (238-269, only for already-exited processes). All three callers (tools/orchestration/stages.py:25-26, pipelines/shared/inference/inference_scheduler.py:91-92, pipelines/tuning/pipeline.py:93-94) invoke `queue.run(jobs)` bare, with no outer try/finally and no process-group kill, so there is no compensating cleanup upstream. A concrete reachable trigger: `_publish_progress` (line 371) -> `GpuProgressFile.write` (185-191) -> `FileIO.save_json(..., atomic=True)` (tools/data/io.py:20-31), which does an unguarded open/json.dump/os.replace; on ENOSPC or a read-only/NFS-stalled run directory it raises OSError that propagates out of the while loop. `_launch` itself can raise OSError (EMFILE, ENOSPC on the log open, ENOMEM at fork) after earlier workers are already in `self.running`. Because CPython's `Popen.__del__` only emits a ResourceWarning and never kills, the already-launched training workers survive the scheduler's death and keep occupying GPUs with no reaper, no progress file, and no results. Adversarial checks that failed to refute: the signal path is genuinely correct (terminate -> wait -> kill -> close -> sys.exit), and `_reconcile` guards its own parse/IO errors inside `GpuPoolFile.requested`, but neither covers a non-signal exception. tests/orchestration/test_gpu_queue.py covers signal-handler restoration and SIGTERM teardown but has no test asserting behavior when an exception escapes the loop, so no test encodes this as intended. This is not one of the listed deliberate orchestration designs.
correction: Two details are off. (1) The anchor line should be run()'s finally at gpu_queue.py:375-376, not 319; line 319 is only the narrow Popen-failure sub-case. (2) The leaked file handle is the trivial half — the scheduler process is exiting, so the OS reclaims the fd. The load-bearing consequence is orphaned training subprocesses left running unsupervised on the GPUs (no reaper, no results JSON, GPU memory held), which is what a `finally` that terminates `self.running` and closes each `log_fh` would fix, along with wrapping the open/Popen pair in _launch so the handle is closed if Popen raises. Severity minor is fair since the trigger is an unexpected OSError on a cold path, though the blast radius (multi-GPU training workers running unattended) is what makes it worth fixing.

title: QueuedInferenceStage._include_item is a hook nothing overrides
description: `_include_item` always returns True and is not overridden by any subclass (checked pipelines/benchmark/stages.py, pipelines/cross_validation/stages.py, pipelines/patch_sweep/stages.py, and the tests). It threads an unused filter through `run()` where it would, if ever used, silently drop the excluded items from both `results` and the written `inference_results.json` with no log line. The sibling hooks `_worker_flag`/`_worker_value` (lines 60-63) are likewise never overridden — every production stage replaces `_job` wholesale.
evidence:
def _include_item(self, item: str) -> bool:
        return True
suggested_fix: Delete the hook and use `self.items` directly, or, if the extension point is wanted, log the excluded items and record them with an EXCLUDED status.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. tools/orchestration/stages.py:157 defines `_include_item` returning a bare True, called only at line 211. A whole-repo grep with no include filter (covering tests/, main/, webui/static/js, and all JSON registries) returns exactly those two hits — no override, no string dispatch, no test. The only QueuedInferenceStage subclasses are pipelines/benchmark/stages.py:296 (InferenceStage) and pipelines/cross_validation/stages.py:49 (FoldInferenceStage); neither overrides it, and FoldInferenceStage overrides run() wholesale so it never even reaches line 211. The described silent-drop consequence is real: `eligible` gates skipped/cached/pending and line 230 re-orders against `eligible`, so an excluded item disappears from both `results` and inference_results.json, with no log line — unlike `skipped`, which gets an explicit warning at line 217. The sibling-hook remark is also factually right that nothing overrides `_worker_flag`/`_worker_value` and that every production stage replaces `_job` (benchmark _seed_command at 288/301, cross_validation --fold at 38, patch_sweep --unit at 36, plus FoldInferenceStage._split_job). This is not one of the listed known non-issues, and it is not a symbol-grep-only inference: the class hierarchy is fully enumerable and the hook is plain Python method resolution, not dynamic dispatch.
correction: The claim lumps `_worker_flag`/`_worker_value` in with `_include_item`, but they are not equivalent. Those two feed the base `QueuedStage._job`, which is unreached in production yet is test-covered: tests/orchestration/test_stages.py:171-182 (test_training_job_command_carries_run_metadata) instantiates QueuedTrainingStage directly and asserts `"--model" in job.command`. So removing them means touching that test. `_include_item` at line 157 is the only genuinely inert member — no override, no caller that can vary its result, no test. Line number and severity in the claim are correct.

title: Interpreter PRIORITY prefers two conda env names that exist nowhere else in the project
description: `PRIORITY` ranks `conda:dlr-cu12` above `conda:Dune` and adds `conda:nazaria`. Grepping the whole repo (py/md/toml/txt/sh) shows `dlr-cu12` and `nazaria` appear only on this line, while `Dune` is the pinned project env everywhere else: `run.sh` probes `$HOME/miniconda3/envs/Dune/bin/python` first, webui/README.md line 14 states "run.sh auto-selects the `Dune` conda interpreter", and the dependency pins target Dune. If an env named `dlr-cu12` happens to exist on a machine, every launched job silently runs under it in preference to the project env, with no indication in the UI beyond the interpreter string.
suggested_fix: Reduce PRIORITY to the env the project actually pins (`conda:Dune`), or document the other two if they are still live on a specific machine.
verdict_notes:
The quoted line is exact: `/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/webui/project_paths.py:9` reads `PRIORITY = ["conda:dlr-cu12", "conda:Dune", "conda:nazaria"]`, and `preferred_interpreter` (line 171-177) walks it in order, returning the first matching discovered env label.

Grep over the repo (py/md/sh/toml/txt/json, excluding the minified mathjax bundle) confirms `dlr-cu12` and `nazaria` appear ONLY on that line. Everything else pins `Dune`: `webui/run.sh` probes `$HOME/miniconda3/envs/Dune/bin/python` first; `webui/README.md:14` says "run.sh auto-selects the `Dune` conda interpreter"; repo `README.md:26-36` says `conda create -n Dune` and "Keep the name `Dune` unless you have a reason not to"; `pyproject.toml`/`requirements.txt` pin to that env. `stetools` in `SCRIPT_PRIORITY` is by contrast cross-referenced everywhere (configuration/inference/general.py:43, configuration/sar/processing_config.py:122,161, main/processing/generate_tomogram.py), which shows the difference between a live entry and a stale one.

Git provenance makes it clearly accidental rather than designed: the list was `["conda:Dune", "conda:nazaria"]` and commit 4a6219b (2026-06-05, "Add detach option, console tiling, tensorboard view…") inserted `conda:dlr-cu12` ABOVE `Dune` as a drive-by edit inside an unrelated webui feature commit. It has never been referenced since.

Concrete failure: `discover_interpreters` enumerates every env under `~/miniconda3|anaconda3|.conda/envs`. On any machine carrying a `dlr-cu12` env, every webui default resolves to it instead of the project env — `/api/run` when the client omits `interpreter` (request_router.py:566), plus paths with no interpreter UI at all: config introspection for `/api/scripts/<key>/config` (line 485, which subprocesses the interpreter to read the config dataclasses), `/api/tensorboard/logdirs` (528-529), tensorboard start and autostart (734, 766). A stale cu12 env against `torch==2.11.0` (README: reference machine is the cu130 build) means wrong deps or a failed config resolve. Meanwhile `run.sh` starts the console itself under Dune, so the console would be running under one env and spawning its children under another — an internal contradiction, not a deliberate machine split.

No test covers `preferred_interpreter` or `PRIORITY` (tests/webui only touches `ProjectPaths` for layout/descriptions/fit_lab/model_probe), so nothing encodes this ordering as intended. None of the KNOWN NON-ISSUES apply.
correction:
Three refinements to the auditor's write-up:

1. Conditional, not currently firing. This machine's envs are Dune, fb, Mercado, nazaria, routing-ppo, Shrimp, worcap — there is no `dlr-cu12`, so today the lookup falls through to `conda:Dune` and behaves correctly. The defect is latent (any machine that grows a `dlr-cu12` env silently flips), which is why minor is the right severity rather than major.

2. `nazaria` is the sharper half of the finding and the auditor understates it. Unlike `dlr-cu12`, that env DOES exist locally and belongs to an unrelated project. It sits third, so if `Dune` were ever renamed or absent the console would silently launch TomoSAR training under a foreign env rather than failing loudly — a silent fallback, which the project's "no legacy fallbacks" policy treats as a finding in its own right.

3. "no indication in the UI beyond the interpreter string" is overstated for the launch and ablation views, which preselect and display `label · path` (static/js/launch.js:606-612, ablation.js:128-134) so a user can see and override it. It is fully accurate for the server-side callers, which have no picker at all: request_router.py:485 (config resolution), 528-529 (tensorboard logdirs), 734 and 766 (tensorboard start/autostart).

Provenance worth adding to the fix note: `git log -S` shows the offending entry entered in commit 4a6219b as an unrelated drive-by; the fix is to restore `PRIORITY = ["conda:Dune"]` (dropping both `dlr-cu12` and `nazaria`) so the console matches run.sh and the READMEs, and to let the existing `interpreters[0]` / `sys.executable` tail handle the no-match case.

title: `get_script` returns an `essentials` field that is always empty and unread
description: `ScriptCatalog.get_script` emits `"essentials": meta.get("essentials", [])`, but no entry in `ScriptCatalog.META` defines an `essentials` key, so the value is always `[]`. The frontend never reads it either: every `essentials` reference in `webui/static/js/launch_widgets.js` (lines 4550, 4554, 4580-4602, 5137) reads `layout.essentials`, which comes from `LaunchLayout.LAYOUTS` via `/api/scripts/<key>/config`, not from the script detail payload.
suggested_fix: Drop the `essentials` key from the `get_script` payload.
verdict_notes:
Reproduced independently.

1. `/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/webui/script_catalog.py:320` emits `"essentials": meta.get("essentials", [])` inside `ScriptCatalog.get_script`.
2. `meta` is `self.META.get(key, {...})`. I parsed `ScriptCatalog.META` with an AST walk: 39 entries, none of them contains an `essentials` key (`entries: 39 with essentials: []`). `META` is never mutated anywhere in the repo (only reads at script_catalog.py:281 and tests/webui/test_launch_layout.py:220). So the field is unconditionally `[]`.
3. A repo-wide grep for `essentials` (py/js/json/html) yields exactly three sites: script_catalog.py:320, `webui/launch_layout.py` (the `LAYOUTS` spec entries plus `build()` at 1551/1561/1579/1649), and `webui/static/js/launch_widgets.js` (4550/4554/4580/4581/4602/5137). Nothing in tests/, main/, or any JSON registry.
4. The frontend references are all `layout.essentials`, where `layout = cfg.layout` (launch_widgets.js:4563) and `cfg` is the response of `GET /api/scripts/<key>/config` — request_router.py:480-491 builds that payload as `{**resolver.resolve(...), "layout": self.layout.build(...)}`, i.e. from `LaunchLayout`, not from the catalog detail.
5. The only consumer of `get_script` is request_router.py:498 (`GET /api/scripts/<key>`), whose payload is consumed by `launch.js:206` and `ablation.js:44`; neither reads `detail.essentials`, and grep finds no `.essentials` access on any script-detail object.
6. No test references `get_script` or `essentials`, so nothing encodes an intent to keep the key.

Not covered by any known non-issue: this is not a dynamic-dispatch registry lookup (the key would have to exist in META to ever be non-empty), and the frontend path is fully accounted for. It is a vestigial always-empty field in an API payload — cosmetic dead code, hence minor. Cited line and mechanism are accurate.

title: `script_entry("args")` and the redundant `"file"` overrides are dead configuration threaded through three call sites
description: `script_entry` exposes `"args": list(override.get("args", []))`, but no entry in `ENTRY_OVERRIDES` defines an `args` key, so the list is always empty; it is nevertheless spliced into `ProcessManager._start` (line 190), `ProcessManager._render_command` (line 306) and `ScriptCatalog.get_script`'s command preview (line 310). Likewise the `"file"` overrides for `cross_validate` (line 61) and `sweep_patches` (line 66) are literally equal to their own keys, so `override.get("file", key)` returns the same value with or without them.
suggested_fix: Remove the `args` plumbing until an entry actually needs extra argv, and drop the two no-op `"file"` entries.
verdict_notes:
Reproduced both halves of the claim directly from source.

1. `args` is always empty. `/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/webui/project_paths.py:140` builds `"args": list(override.get("args", []))` from `ENTRY_OVERRIDES` (lines 15-70). I read the whole dict: all 13 entries define only `config_module`, `config_class`, and (twice) `file`. No entry defines `args`, and nothing anywhere mutates `ENTRY_OVERRIDES` (repo-wide grep for `ENTRY_OVERRIDES` hits only its definition and the `.get` at line 132). So `entry["args"]` is unconditionally `[]`.

The three consumers confirmed:
- `webui/process_manager.py:190` — `argv = [record["interpreter"], "-u", str(entry["path"]), *entry["args"]]`
- `webui/process_manager.py:306` — `parts = [interpreter, "-u", entry["rel"], *entry["args"]]`
- `webui/script_catalog.py:310` — `command = " ".join(["python", spec["rel"], *spec["args"]])`
Each splices an always-empty list, so the key contributes nothing to any command line or preview.

I checked the dynamic-dispatch escape hatches the protocol warns about: no `/api` payload, no `webui/static/js` code, and no JSON registry supplies `args` (the only JS matches were `webui/tools/visual/node_modules/playwright-core` noise). The four webui test stubs (`tests/webui/test_process_manager_gpu_pool.py:60`, `test_saved_run_store.py:44`, `test_process_manager_queue.py:36`, `test_process_manager_progress.py:36`) all hardcode `"args": []` as well, so no test exercises a non-empty value either — the tests encode the key as pure ceremony, not as covered behavior.

2. The `"file"` overrides are self-referential. Line 133 is `file_stem = override.get("file", key)`. For `"cross_validate"` the override sets `"file": "cross_validate"` (line 61) and for `"sweep_patches"` it sets `"file": "sweep_patches"` (line 66) — both literally equal their own dict keys, so removing them changes nothing. Note the `file` *mechanism* itself is not dead (it is the default-to-key path used by every other entry); only those two explicit overrides are redundant.

This is genuinely unused configuration plumbing, not dynamic dispatch I failed to trace. It is cosmetic — there is no behavioral failure, no wrong command is ever built — so `minor` is the right severity, matching the auditor's call.
correction: Details are accurate as filed (file, line 140, and the two `file` overrides at lines 61 and 66 all check out). Two refinements worth carrying into the report: (a) the `override.get("file", key)` mechanism at line 133 is NOT dead — it is the fallback every other entry relies on; only the two self-equal `"file"` values are redundant, so a fix should delete those two lines and keep line 133; (b) the four webui test stubs also hardcode `"args": []`, so removing the key requires updating `tests/webui/test_process_manager_gpu_pool.py:60`, `test_saved_run_store.py:44`, `test_process_manager_queue.py:36`, and `test_process_manager_progress.py:36` in the same change.

title: `unquote` is imported but never used; percent-encoded static/media paths are never decoded
description: `unquote` is imported from `urllib.parse` and never called anywhere in the module (verified by grepping all of webui/). Consequently `_serve_static` passes the raw, still-encoded path segment to the filesystem, so any request for a static asset containing a percent-escape (a space, a `#`, a non-ASCII character) 404s. No current asset under `webui/static/` has such a name, so the effect is latent, but the unused import is evidence the decoding step was intended and dropped.
evidence: from urllib.parse import parse_qs, unquote, urlparse
suggested_fix: Either apply `unquote` to the relative path in `_serve_static`/`_serve_results_media`, or delete the import.
verdict_notes:
Reproduced from source. A repo-wide grep (`grep -rn "unquote" --include=*` over the entire tree, including tests/, main/, webui/static/js, and all *.json registries) returns exactly one hit: the import statement itself at webui/request_router.py:10. `unquote` is a stdlib free function, not a registry-dispatched symbol, so the "dynamic dispatch" caveat does not rescue it — the import is genuinely unused.

The decoding gap the auditor infers is also real in principle. webui/web_ui_server.py:49 defines `_Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler)`, not `SimpleHTTPRequestHandler` — the latter is the class that calls `unquote` inside its own `translate_path`. So `handler.path` arrives percent-encoded, `route()` (line 981) takes `urlparse(handler.path).path` which preserves escapes, and `_serve_static` (line 961) builds `(self.paths.static_dir / relative).resolve()` from the still-encoded segment. A GET for `/static/js/my%20file.js` would stat a file literally named `my%20file.js` and 404 at line 967.

The effect is unreachable today: `find` over webui/static/ shows no filename containing a space, `#`, or any non-ASCII byte, and every asset reference in index.html is plain ASCII with only a `?v=` cache-buster that urlparse strips before routing. There is no test exercising `_serve_static`; the only request_router test is tests/webui/test_request_router_jsonsafe.py, which covers `_jsonsafe` only.

Not a KNOWN NON-ISSUE: this is not a deferred import in main/, not a legacy-fallback question, and not one of the listed deliberate quirks. Confirmed as dead code, minor.
correction: Two details in the claim are off. (1) The title's "static/media paths" overstates the scope: `_serve_results_media` is NOT affected, because it receives its path from `parse_qs(urlparse(handler.path).query)` and `parse_qs` already percent-decodes its values. Only `_serve_static` consumes a raw path segment. (The same raw-path extraction also feeds `/api/scripts/<key>`, `/api/backbones/<key>/note`, and `/api/jobs/<id>/...`, but those keys are ASCII identifiers, so nothing is reachable there either.) (2) The residual finding is the unused import alone; the 404 behaviour is unreachable with the current asset set, so it should be described as latent rather than as a bug. Note for the fix: inserting `unquote` in `_serve_static` is safe because the `resolve()` + `is_relative_to` guard at lines 962-965 runs after path construction, so decoding cannot open a traversal hole.

title: Ready banner and all background monitors start before the socket is bound
description: `serve()` prints the "DLR-TomoSAR Control Console / URL http://host:port" banner and starts the resource watchdog, contention monitor, GPU watchdog, GPU schedule and progress watcher threads, and only then constructs `_Server((self.host, self.port), _Handler)`. If the port is already taken (a second console, or a stale detached instance — a routine situation given the detach feature) the operator sees a successful-looking banner advertising a URL that belongs to the *other* process, followed by an `OSError: Address already in use` traceback. The GPU-schedule and GPU-watchdog threads also get a window in which they can act on shared state for a server that will never serve.
suggested_fix: Construct and bind `_Server` first, then start the monitor threads and print the banner.
verdict_notes:
The ordering in the claim is exactly what the source does, and I reproduced the failure end-to-end.

/home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/webui/web_ui_server.py:147-159 — `serve()` calls `self._report_ready()` (line 148, which logs the "DLR-TomoSAR Control Console" banner including `URL http://{host}:{port}`, lines 170-181), then starts watchdog/contention/gpu_guard/gpu_schedule/progress_watch threads (149-153), and only at line 155 constructs `_Server((self.host, self.port), _Handler)`. `_Server` subclasses `ThreadingHTTPServer`, so `socketserver.TCPServer.__init__` binds with `bind_and_activate=True`; `HTTPServer.allow_reuse_address = 1` sets SO_REUSEADDR, which on Linux does NOT permit a second listener on an already-listening address (that would need SO_REUSEPORT), so EADDRINUSE is raised.

No caller guards the port: webui/serve.py:19-22 just builds `WebUIServer(host, port)` and calls `serve()`; webui/run.sh execs serve.py with no pre-check or pre-kill of an existing console; ServerDetacher (webui/process_manager.py:861+) has no port-ownership handshake, so a detached stale instance keeps the port. Grep found no `allow_reuse_address` override, port probe, or bind precheck anywhere.

Empirical reproduction (Dune env, port pre-bound by a helper socket): stdout printed the full banner with `URL http://127.0.0.1:60691`, plus "resource watchdog armed", "contention monitor armed", "gpu watchdog armed", "gpu schedule armed ... (enabled=True, greedy=True, charity=False)", followed by `OSError: [Errno 98] Address already in use` at web_ui_server.py:155, exit code 1. The advertised URL in that banner belongs to the other process.

Tests do not encode the opposite behavior: the only test touching this path is /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/tests/webui/test_server_detach.py, which always picks a free port (`_free_port`) and polls until /api/jobs answers, so it never exercises the conflict.

On the secondary "threads act on shared state" part: ResourceWatchdog, ContentionMonitor, GpuWatchdog and ExperimentProgressWatcher all `time.sleep(INTERVAL)` before their first evaluation (4-10 s), so they cannot act in the millisecond window. GpuSchedule is the exception — webui/gpu_schedule.py:421-433 runs `tick()`/`charity()`/`sweep()` immediately and only then sleeps, so it can genuinely touch gpu_pool.json / schedule state on behalf of a server that will never serve. That is a real but narrow race, not the main harm.

Two refinements to the mechanism: (1) all monitors except GpuSchedule sleep their full interval before the first tick (ResourceWatchdog 5 s, ContentionMonitor 5 s, GpuWatchdog 4 s, ExperimentProgressWatcher 10 s), so only GpuSchedule (webui/gpu_schedule.py:421-433 ticks before sleeping) can actually mutate shared state in the window before the bind raises; the auditor's "GPU-watchdog threads also get a window" is overstated. (2) The `finally` cleanup at lines 165-168 also never runs, since the exception fires before the `try`, though that is harmless here (nothing was bound and TensorBoard was not started). Fix is to construct/bind `_Server` first and only then report ready and start the monitors.

title: self.applied is mutated by the watcher thread without the lock while state() iterates it
description: `self.lock` guards `settings`, `nap_until`, `gifted` and `last_charity`, but `self.applied` is read and written entirely outside it: the watcher thread assigns `self.applied[job_id] = {...}` per job and rebinds the whole dict in `tick` (lines 270 and 277), `_cross` writes `["withheld"]` (242), `_donate` appends to a `withheld` list (335) and `sweep` rewrites it (410). Meanwhile `state()`, called from every `/api/system` request thread, iterates `self.applied.values()` and each `record["withheld"]` list. An interleaving there raises "dictionary changed size during iteration" / "list changed size during iteration" and 500s the whole system endpoint.
evidence: waiting = sorted({gpu for record in self.applied.values() for gpu in record["withheld"]})
suggested_fix: Bring `self.applied` under `self.lock` (or take a snapshot copy of it inside the lock at the top of `state()`), consistent with how the rest of the mutable state in this class is handled.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/webui/gpu_schedule.py:156 creates `self.lock`, and every accessor of `settings`, `nap_until`, `gifted`, `last_charity` takes it (lines 202, 219, 233, 260, 282, 342, 354, 386, 441, 474). `self.applied` (line 158) is never touched under that lock: the watcher thread writes it at 242 (`_cross`), 270 and 277 (`tick`), 335 (`_donate`) and 410 (`sweep`); `_watch` (421-433) runs `tick`/`charity`/`sweep` on a daemon thread every 30 s (started at 435-437). `state()` reads it unsynchronized at line 450: `waiting = sorted({gpu for record in self.applied.values() for gpu in record["withheld"]})`. `state()` is reached from `/api/system` (webui/request_router.py:546) and from `update()` (line 485, POST handler at request_router.py:610); the server is `ThreadingHTTPServer` with `daemon_threads = True` (webui/web_ui_server.py:43-46, 158), and webui/static/js/home.js:182 polls `/api/system` on a timer, so multiple independent threads can be inside `state()` while the watcher ticks. `route()` catches the exception and answers 500 (request_router.py:996-1001), so the concrete failure is: a new live job appears, the watcher executes `self.applied[job_id] = {...}` at line 270 (a dict insertion, size change) while a poll thread is mid-iteration over `self.applied.values()` at line 450 → `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` → the whole /api/system payload 500s (home dashboard blanks for that poll). tests/webui/test_gpu_schedule.py drives `tick`/`sweep`/`state` single-threaded only (e.g. lines 177, 234, 247, 260, 279, 339 assert on `scheduler.applied` directly), so nothing encodes lock-free access as intended design — the omission of `applied` from the lock's coverage looks like an oversight, not a decision. Not one of the listed known non-issues (the charity/greedy/intrusion semantics are deliberate; this is about the mutex scope, not the policy).
correction: The mechanism is real but narrower than the auditor states. (1) The only interleaving that can actually raise is the dict insertion of a *new* job_id at line 270 while a reader iterates `self.applied.values()`. Rebinding the whole dict at line 277 (`self.applied = {...}`) does NOT affect an in-flight iteration — the reader holds a reference to the old dict object — and there is no in-place `del`, so shrink cannot trigger it either. (2) "list changed size during iteration" is not a real Python failure: lists have no mutation guard, so the `record["withheld"].append(gpu)` at line 335 racing the inner `for gpu in record["withheld"]` yields duplicated/short reads at worst, never an exception. Likewise line 242 and line 410 rebind the `withheld` key (atomic assignment), so a reader sees either the old or the new list, not a corrupt one. So the confirmed defect is a single unsynchronized dict-mutation race with a very small window (a few-entry iteration vs. one insertion per newly-started live job), whose blast radius is one transient 500 that the next poll recovers from. Fix: take `self.lock` around the `self.applied` mutations in `tick`/`_cross`/`_donate`/`sweep` and around the line-450 read (or snapshot `list(self.applied.values())` plus `list(record["withheld"])` under the lock). Minor severity is correct.

title: I/O danger level is thresholded with the memory PSI constant
description: The escalation from "warn" to "danger" for disk contention compares the I/O full-pressure average against `MEM_PSI_FULL`, a constant named and documented for memory pressure; there is no `IO_PSI_FULL`. The class already keeps separate `MEM_PSI_SOME`, `IO_PSI_SOME`, `CPU_PSI_SOME` and a separate `IO_UTIL`, so this reads as a copy-paste from the memory block two lines above. It matters because "danger" is the level that `_check_nuke` (line 405) counts towards firing auto-nuke on the user's own jobs.
suggested_fix: Introduce an explicit `IO_PSI_FULL` class constant with the intended value and use it here, so the I/O escalation threshold is tunable independently of the memory one.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. webui/contention_monitor.py:381 reads `io_level = "danger" if psi["io"]["full"] >= self.MEM_PSI_FULL else "warn"`, and a repo-wide grep for `PSI_FULL` returns only three hits: the definition `MEM_PSI_FULL = 3.0` (line 19), the memory escalation (line 371), and this I/O escalation (line 381). No `IO_PSI_FULL` exists. The class otherwise tunes every threshold per resource (MEM_PSI_SOME=10, IO_PSI_SOME=25, CPU_PSI_SOME=40, plus a dedicated IO_UTIL=80), so a deliberately shared full-stall threshold would have been named PSI_FULL rather than referenced through the memory-specific name. The consequence path the auditor cites is real: _track("io", io_level, ...) -> _raise stores the level in self.active["io"] -> _check_nuke (line 405) selects entries with mine and level == "danger" and kind != "leak", so a disk alarm with mine_share >= SHARE can accumulate the NUKE_SUSTAIN streak that calls self.nuke.nuke() on the user's own jobs. No test covers ContentionMonitor (grep for the class name and "contention" over tests/ returns nothing), so nothing encodes contrary intent. This is not one of the listed known non-issues. Concrete failure: tuning MEM_PSI_FULL for memory behaviour silently retunes disk auto-nuke sensitivity — e.g. raising it to 8.0 to suppress memory false alarms also makes I/O contention three times harder to escalate to "danger", changing whether auto-nuke fires on a disk-bound job, with nothing in the name or the state() limits payload to reveal the coupling. Conversely, at the current 3.0 the I/O "some" breach bar is 2.5x memory's while the full bar is identical, so I/O escalates to "danger" disproportionately easily relative to the memory block it was copied from. I could not prove the numeric value 3.0 is wrong for I/O in absolute terms — PSI full avg10 is dimensionally the same quantity for both resources — so the defect is the cross-resource constant coupling and misnamed reference, not a demonstrably wrong number.
correction: Line, file, and severity are correct. Refine the mechanism: the demonstrable defect is latent tuning coupling plus a misnamed reference, not a value that is provably wrong at runtime. PSI "full" avg10 is the same dimensionless stall percentage for memory and I/O, so 3.0 is not absurd for disk; what is broken is that the I/O escalation has no threshold of its own, so any future adjustment of MEM_PSI_FULL silently changes disk auto-nuke sensitivity, and the asymmetry (IO_PSI_SOME is 2.5x MEM_PSI_SOME while the full bar is shared) makes I/O reach "danger" disproportionately easily. Also worth noting for the fix: state() publishes mem_psi_some/io_psi_some/cpu_psi_some but no full threshold at all, and there is zero test coverage for ContentionMonitor anywhere under tests/, so adding an IO_PSI_FULL constant carries no test-breakage risk and should be accompanied by exposing the full thresholds in the limits payload.

title: ContentionMonitor.state() serializes an `impacting` flag and a `limits` block that nothing consumes
description: `impacting`, the whole `limits` dict (mem_psi_some, io_psi_some, cpu_psi_some, load_ratio, swap_out_mbs, share, interval, nuke_after_s) and `nuke_streak` are built on every `/api/system` poll but no consumer exists: grepping the entire repo (webui/static/js, *.html, tests, JSON registries) finds these key names only in this file. title: GPU history series desynchronise from the CPU/RAM series when nvidia-smi hiccups
description: `sample()` always appends one CPU and one RAM sample, but appends to the per-GPU tracks only for the devices `_gpu_devices()` returned; that helper returns `[]` on a non-zero exit, a timeout or an OSError. After any transient failure the GPU deques are permanently shorter than the CPU/RAM deques, yet `state()` publishes a single `period_s`/`max_samples` pair and home.js plots all series against that shared time axis (home.js:609-611, 623-635). The GPU sparkline then shows samples shifted in time relative to the CPU/RAM sparklines, with nothing indicating the gap. Stale tracks for devices that disappear are also never removed from `self.gpus`.
suggested_fix: Append a placeholder (or a None the frontend can render as a gap) to every known GPU track when the device list comes back empty or short, so all series stay index-aligned.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. webui/system_monitor.py:392-405 (`SystemHistory.sample`) appends one CPU and one RAM sample unconditionally, but appends to per-GPU tracks only for the devices returned by `SystemMonitor._gpu_devices()` (lines 135-163), which returns `[]` on OSError, `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` (3s timeout, called every 0.5s from `sample_loop`) or a non-zero exit, and also `continue`s past any CSV line with <9 cells. `state()` (407-415) publishes a single `period_s`/`max_samples` for all series. On the frontend, home.js:611 sets `this.histMax = hist.max_samples` and `_spark` (line 1177) uses `const step = w / (this.histMax - 1)` with `x0 = w - (d.length - 1) * step`, i.e. a fixed pixel-per-sample step with right alignment for every series. So a GPU track that missed k samples has each of its points drawn k*0.5s too recent relative to the CPU/RAM sparkline, with no indication of the gap. Note home.js never reads `period_s` at all — only `max_samples` — so the shared axis is the fixed step. Tests (tests/webui/test_system_history.py) stub `_gpu_devices` to a constant 2-device list and never exercise the empty/partial return, so intended behaviour is not encoded against the claim. This is not one of the known non-issues.
correction: Two details of the mechanism are off. (1) "GPU deques are permanently shorter" is wrong: all deques have maxlen=MAX_SAMPLES=144, so ~72s after a hiccup the GPU deque is 144 long again and lengths match. What actually persists is the time-axis distortion — the GPU's 144 samples span 144+k sample periods of wall clock yet are plotted over the same 144-step axis, so the GPU trace is time-compressed/shifted relative to CPU/RAM, cumulatively with each dropped sample. (2) The stale-track half has no UI effect: home.js iterates `gpus.forEach((g, i)) => gpuHist[String(i)]`, so orphan keys in `self.gpus` are simply never read (wasted memory only). The sharper defect on line 400 is that tracks are keyed by `enumerate` position instead of device uuid/index: if one device is missing from a single nvidia-smi listing (empty return, or the <9-cell `continue` in `_gpu_devices`), the following devices shift down a position and their samples are appended to another card's history track, silently mixing two GPUs' data in one series.

title: Runs-root sets are mutated by one request thread while another iterates them
description: `self.roots` is a plain `set` populated by the listing endpoints and iterated by the validation helpers from other request threads. The server is a `ThreadingHTTPServer` (web_ui_server.py:43-46), so a `/api/cubes?base=...` call that runs `self.roots.add(str(root))` (cube_explorer.py:133) concurrently with a `/api/cubes/slice` call iterating `self.roots` in `_stamp_dir` can raise `RuntimeError: Set changed size during iteration`. The same pattern exists in webui/results_browser.py (add at line 46, iterate at line 119), webui/run_leaderboard.py (add at lines 110 and 211, iterate at line 380) and webui/training_curves.py (add at line 26, iterate at line 115). It surfaces as a spurious 500 when the user reopens the Results tab while another panel is loading.
evidence: if not any(stamp_dir.is_relative_to(root) for root in self.roots):
suggested_fix: Guard the roots set with the existing lock, or iterate a snapshot (`for root in tuple(self.roots)`), or replace the set with a frozenset swapped atomically on update.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. webui/web_ui_server.py defines `_Server(ThreadingHTTPServer)` with `daemon_threads = True` and constructs a single shared `CubeExplorer`/`ResultsBrowser`/`RunLeaderboard`/`TrainingCurves` handed to one `RequestRouter`, so request handler threads share these objects. In cube_explorer.py, `self.roots = set()` (line 123) is unsynchronised — the adjacent `self.lock` (line 124) guards only `self.loaded` (used at lines 826 and in the load worker), never `roots`. `list_cubes` mutates it with `self.roots.add(str(root))` (line 133) from a `/api/cubes` thread, while `_stamp_dir` iterates it in a generator expression `any(stamp_dir.is_relative_to(root) for root in self.roots)` (line 836, exactly as quoted) from a `/api/cubes/slice` thread. `Path.is_relative_to` is pure-Python and spans many bytecodes, so a thread switch mid-iteration is possible; if the concurrent `add` inserts a root not already present, CPython raises `RuntimeError: Set changed size during iteration`. `RequestRouter.route` (request_router.py:996-999) catches all exceptions and replies with HTTP 500 plus the exception text, so it surfaces as a spurious 500. The four sibling sites are also as claimed: results_browser.py 35/46/119, run_leaderboard.py 103/110/211/380, training_curves.py 18/26/115. Frontend JS confirms genuinely concurrent callers exist (tomogram.js:1358 `/api/cubes` and tomogram.js:2132 `/api/cubes/slice`; slice_collector.js:70 and triage.js:52 also hit `/api/cubes`; leaderboard.js drives both `/api/leaderboard` and `/api/curves*`). No test covers concurrent access — tests/webui/test_slice_collector.py:56 only pins the path-containment security behaviour. This is not any of the listed known non-issues.
correction: Two details are off. (1) The auditor missed a fifth site: cube_explorer.py:1451, where `SliceCollector` iterates another object's set — `matches = [root for root in self.cubes.roots if stamp_dir.is_relative_to(root)]` — while `/api/cubes` mutates `CubeExplorer.roots`; this is the cross-component instance of the same race. (2) The stated trigger is wrong and overstates the likelihood: re-adding a root already in the set does not change its size and cannot raise `RuntimeError`, so "reopening the Results tab while another panel is loading" (which re-adds the same path) is normally harmless. The error requires a genuinely NEW root string to be inserted during another thread's iteration over a set that typically holds 1-3 entries, i.e. changing the runs-directory base while slice/curve requests are in flight — a window of microseconds. Real defect, but the practical hit rate is far lower than described. Fix is a one-line `threading.Lock` (or snapshotting `tuple(self.roots)` before iterating) at each of the five sites.

title: features_png has an unreachable-and-broken fallback branch for non-3D activation maps
description: Line 323 already returns `None` when `stored.ndim < 4`, so `maps = stored[0]` always has `ndim >= 3`. For the normal 4-D activation case `maps.ndim == 3` and `energy` is never `None`, which makes the `else range(min(max_channels, maps.shape[0]))` arm dead. In the only case that could reach it (a 5-D activation, `maps.ndim == 4`), `maps[channel]` would be 3-D and `ax.imshow` would raise. `len(list(order))` is also materialised twice (lines 331 and 342) for a value that never changes.
evidence: order  = np.argsort(energy)[::-1][:max_channels] if energy is not None else range(min(max_channels, maps.shape[0]))
suggested_fix: Replace the guard with an exact `stored.ndim != 4` rejection, drop the `energy is None` branch, and compute the channel list once into a local before using its length.
verdict_notes: Reproduced from source. /home/bard/Bard/code/DLR-TomoSAR/webui/model_probe.py:323 returns None for stored.ndim < 4, so maps = stored[0].numpy() (line 326) always has ndim >= 3. energy (line 327) is None only when maps.ndim != 3, i.e. stored.ndim >= 5. stored comes from ActivationRecorder._store_hook (tools/diagnostics/activation_recorder.py:144-149), which records the first tensor output of LEAF modules only (leaf_names(), line 111), and self.loaded["layers"] (model_probe.py:68) is exactly that leaf list. No leaf module in models/ can emit a 5-D tensor: there is no Conv3d/ConvTranspose3d/BatchNorm3d anywhere in models/, and the 5-/6-D reshapes in models/backbone/swin_unet.py (lines 52-53, 134-183) are intermediates inside container forward bodies, never a leaf module's output. Therefore energy is never None and the `else range(min(max_channels, maps.shape[0]))` arm at line 328 is unreachable. Were it reachable (5-D activation), maps[channel] would be 3-D and ax.imshow at line 338 would raise TypeError: Invalid shape for image data (unless the trailing dim were coincidentally 3 or 4), so the fallback is broken rather than protective — the kind of silent-but-wrong compat arm the project's "break loudly, no legacy fallbacks" policy forbids. No test covers features_png (tests/webui/test_model_probe.py never mentions it); the only caller is webui/request_router.py:228.
correction: Line and mechanism are correct. Two refinements: (1) the double len(list(order)) (lines 331 and 342) is duplication but not an efficiency issue — order holds at most max_channels=16 entries and features_png is a cold, user-triggered PNG render, so treat it as cosmetic tidy-up, not part of the defect; (2) the adjacent stored.ndim < 4 guard at line 323 also returns None silently instead of surfacing an error, so if this is fixed, the right shape is to drop the else arm and let the unsupported-rank case fail (or report) explicitly rather than adding a second silent None path.
